articles.title: ILEARN International Limited to be wound up following resolutions
articles.excerpt: ILEARN International Limited, based in Rochdale, has passed resolutions for voluntary winding-up, appointing a liquidator to oversee the process.
articles.content_html:
ILEARN International Limited, located at Globe House, Globe Park, Moss Bridge Road, Rochdale, has passed resolutions for voluntary winding-up as of 4 November 2026.

The company, which also operated from the Chadderton & Learning Development Centre in Oldham, appointed Peter John Harold of Bespoke Insolvency Solutions as liquidator for the process.

Peter Harold can be contacted for further details via email at info@bespokeinsolvency.co.uk. Mark Gandy is listed as an alternative contact.

This development follows a formal notice published in The Gazette on 12 November 2026, indicating the company's decision to cease operations.

articles.content_html:
Sanderson's Floor & Roof Truss Company Limited, based at 179 Milnrow Road, Rochdale, has entered liquidation as of 12 November 2026, according to an official notice in The Gazette.

The company, which specialised in the manufacture of builders carpentry and joinery, has appointed Richard Ian Williamson and Francesca Vivace from Xeinadin Corporate Recovery as liquidators.

This development may impact employees and suppliers connected to the business, as the liquidation process unfolds.

The company, registered under number 07093695, has faced financial difficulties leading to this decision, marking a significant change in its operations.

articles.excerpt: iREEF, a Rochdale-based aquatic retailer, has been awarded Marine Fish Retailer of the Year in Practical Fishkeeping's annual Readers' Poll.
articles.content_html:
iREEF, a shop located in Rochdale, has been awarded the title of Marine Fish Retailer of the Year for 2026 as part of Practical Fishkeeping's annual Readers' Poll.

The Readers' Poll featured an alphabetical list of 40 aquatic retailers, with iREEF standing out for its commitment to customer satisfaction and community engagement.

articles.content_html:

The award highlights the takeaway's commitment to quality food and its strong reputation in a competitive culinary market. River Beal Takeaway has won two awards this year, further establishing its status in the region.

The owners of River Beal Takeaway expressed pride in their achievement, noting that the recognition reflects their dedication to providing excellent service and food quality.

The Euro Asia Curry Awards celebrate the best in the culinary field across the UK, and River Beal's win is part of a national recognition of outstanding takeaways.

articles.excerpt: North West Removals and Storage Limited, based at Unit 5c, Gorrels Way, Rochdale, has passed resolutions to wind up the company voluntarily as of 6 November 2026. The resolutions were made during a meeting where Daniel Ormerod and Lauren Fitton of Leonard Curtis were appointed as joint liquidators to manage the winding-up process.
articles.content_html:
North West Removals and Storage Limited, based at Unit 5c, Gorrels Way, Rochdale, has passed resolutions to wind up the company voluntarily as of 6 November 2026. The decision was made during a meeting held on 6 November 2026.

Daniel Ormerod and Lauren Fitton of Leonard Curtis have been appointed as joint liquidators to oversee the winding-up process. Their role will involve managing the dissolution of the company and addressing any outstanding matters related to its closure.

The company also operated from additional addresses in Haslingden and Accrington, which may affect its operations and obligations in those areas as well.

This development may impact employees and creditors of North West Removals and Storage Limited as the liquidation process unfolds, with the joint liquidators now responsible for handling the company's affairs.

articles.title: Littleborough pub launches new pool league to strengthen community ties
articles.excerpt: Admiral Taverns pub in Littleborough invites local venues to join a new pool league, fostering community spirit and competition among players.
articles.content_html:
A new pool league has been launched by a pub in Littleborough, aiming to bring local venues together and enhance community spirit.

The initiative, organised by Mark Jones, invites pubs with pool tables to form teams and participate in friendly competition without the need for extensive travel.

The league is designed to encourage participation from various local pubs, allowing players to enjoy the game in a familiar setting. Admiral Taverns, which operates around 1,300 pubs across the UK, supports this initiative as part of its commitment to community building.

In addition to the league, a new ladies' pool team is set to be launched in March or April, further promoting inclusivity and engagement within the local community.

The licensees of the participating pubs believe in the vital role that local pubs play in fostering connections among residents.

The league is currently inviting more venues to enter their own teams, providing an opportunity for local players to enjoy competition while strengthening community ties.

articles.title: Dunelm Rochdale shoppers fill store with Christmas gifts for Delivering Joy appeal
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale store says customers have dropped off so many presents in the past week that staff are preparing a count. Gifts go to local causes for people who might otherwise go without.
articles.content_html:
Shoppers at Dunelm's Rochdale store have dropped off so many Christmas presents for its Delivering Joy appeal that staff are preparing to count them up.

The store has thanked customers for the gifts left over the past week, which will go to people in the community who might otherwise go without at Christmas.

In a message to customers, the Rochdale store said: “We’ve had sooooo many gifts dropped off in store over the past week by lots of lovely customers – thank you so much for taking part, you are all so thoughtful & generous! We can’t wait to do a count up to see how many gifts we have now!”

Delivering Joy, which returned on 13 October, is now in its seventh year. Shoppers pick up a gift tag in store, buy a present and leave it at the store, which passes the gifts on to local causes.

Last year the homeware retailer donated nearly 200,000 gifts to more than 1,500 local causes across its stores, according to Dunelm.

Gift bags must be left unsealed so staff can check the contents before the presents are delivered.

If the tags have run out, shoppers can still take part by donating to Age UK, either online at dunelm.com or in store by taking an Age UK bauble to the till and giving anything from £1 to £100.

Source: Dunelm Rochdale and Dunelm, supplied to Rochdale Daily. Photograph: Dunelm Rochdale.

articles.title: The best beauty salons in Rochdale ranked
articles.excerpt: An aesthetics clinic in Norden tops Rochdale Daily's ranking of 18 beauty salons across the borough, scored from 5,374 Google and Fresha reviews.
articles.content_html:
An aesthetics clinic in Norden tops Rochdale Daily's ranking of 18 beauty salons across the borough, scored from 5,374 public reviews on Google and Fresha.

The Aesthetic Rooms on Edenfield Road scored 92.6 out of 100, narrowly ahead of Elements Health & Beauty in Newhey on 91.4. Bare Beauty and Tanning Boutique in Milnrow was third.

Every salon in the top nine is reviewed on both Google and the booking platform Fresha. The town-centre salons with the most Google reviews, led by Pearls on The Walk, take bookings by phone rather than through Fresha, which is why they sit lower down the table.

The top ten

1. The Aesthetic Rooms, Edenfield Road, Norden: 92.6. Google 5.0 from 112 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 372. An aesthetics clinic offering skin treatments, peels and injectables.

2. Elements Health & Beauty, Shaw Road, Newhey: 91.4. Google 5.0 from 108 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 256. A day spa offering massage, facials and head spa treatments.

3. Bare Beauty and Tanning Boutique, Dale Street, Milnrow: 87.7. Google 4.8 from 43 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 958, the most Fresha reviews of any salon in the table.

4. Be Beau With Grace, Norden: 86.4. Google 4.8 from 44 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 612. Lashes, brows, semi-permanent make-up and training courses.

5. Ella Louise Beautyy, Castleton: 80.1. Google 5.0 from 11 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 130. A home-based nail and beauty studio.

6. ER Beauty Lounge, Halifax Road, Littleborough: 78.0. Google 5.0 from one review; Fresha 5.0 from 730.

7. Beauty by Jemma, Dale Street, Milnrow: 77.0. Google 5.0 from six reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 98.

8. Lush Beauty N Spa, Oldham Road: 75.8. Google 4.7 from 120 reviews; Fresha 5.0 from 13.

9. Olivia Bells Clinic, Halifax Road: 75.4. Google 5.0 from 12 reviews; Fresha 4.9 from 44.

10. Cwbeautyofficial, Dale Street, Milnrow: 47.6. Fresha 5.0 from 418 reviews; no Google listing found.

The rest of the table

11. NailsByAnabelx, Dale Street, Milnrow: 47.3 (Fresha 5.0 from 384; no Google rating).

12. Pearls Hair, Nails & Beauty, The Walk: 47.0 (Google 4.9 from 365, the most Google reviews of any salon in the table; not reviewed on Fresha).

13. Sleek N Chique Beauty & Fashion Salon, Milkstone Place: 45.6 (Google 5.0 from 120).

14. Elegant Beauty and Nails, Sussex Street: 44.8 (Google 5.0 from 97).

15. Nails By Hediye, Yorkshire Street: 41.1 (Google 5.0 from 39).

16. BZ Beauty Studio, Oldham Road: 40.2 (Google 4.8 from 105).

17. Simply Special, Baillie Street: 40.0 (Google 4.9 from 48).

18. Nia Hair & Beauty VIP, Yorkshire Street: 35.8 (Google 4.6 from 128).

How we ranked them

Every figure was taken from the salons' public Google and Fresha listings on Sunday 8 November 2026. No salon was visited, contacted or paid to take part, and none paid to be included.

Each salon could score up to 50 points from Google and up to 50 from Fresha, making 100 in total. Within each half, 30 points are for the star rating and 20 are for the number of reviews.

The rating points are weighted so that a perfect score from a handful of reviews cannot beat a near-perfect score from hundreds. Each salon is treated as if it had 25 extra reviews at the average rating on that platform across the salons in the table: 4.88 stars on Google and 5.00 on Fresha. The more real reviews a salon has, the less those imaginary 25 matter.

The review-count points rise more slowly the more reviews a salon has, so 1,000 reviews is not worth ten times as much as 100. The most-reviewed salon on each platform receives the full 20 points: Pearls on Google, with 365, and Bare Beauty and Tanning Boutique on Fresha, with 958.

A salon not reviewed on one of the two platforms scores nothing for that half. That is the single biggest factor in the table. Pearls, for example, earns 47.0 of a possible 50 Google points, more than any other salon, but scores nothing from Fresha. ER Beauty Lounge has only one Google review but 730 on Fresha, and finishes six places higher.

Fresha's reviews come only from customers who booked through it, and almost every salon there holds a perfect 5.0. Its half of the score therefore reflects how many customers book a salon online more than any difference in rating.

Facebook was left out. Follower figures could not be gathered reliably for every salon, and the size of a page's audience says little about the treatment customers receive.

The ranking covers beauty, nail, skin and spa businesses within Rochdale borough. Hair salons will be ranked separately. Salons in Whitworth and Shawforth carry Rochdale postcodes but sit in Rossendale, so they were not included. Home-based studios are named by area only.

Ratings change daily, and this table records them as they stood on 8 November 2026. Salons that believe a figure is wrong can send a correction, with a link to the listing, to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

Source: Google and Fresha public listings, accessed by Rochdale Daily on 8 November 2026. Image: The Aesthetic Rooms / supplied.

articles.title: How much will Christmas dinner cost in Rochdale? Lidl's £11.11 deal and how rivals compared
articles.excerpt: Lidl is first to price its 2026 Christmas dinner. Here is how it stacks up against last year's Aldi, Tesco and Morrisons deals for a family of four.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale families can buy a basic Christmas dinner for £11.11 at Lidl this year, the first 2026 supermarket price to be announced, with rival deals still to come.

Lidl says its bundle feeds eight for £1.39 a head. For a family of four the shopping list is the same, because the turkey and packs only come in one size, so it works out at about £2.78 each, with leftovers.

The items are on sale in stores from 19 December until Christmas Eve, and Lidl has warned that stock can sell out.

Lidl's basket is a 3kg Birchwood British turkey at £8.85, a 170g pack of sage and onion stuffing at 45p, 15 Yorkshire puddings at 46p and 300g of gravy granules at 99p.

The vegetables are 9p each: 2kg of potatoes, 1kg of carrots, 500g of sprouts and 500g of parsnips. Rochdale Daily has checked that the eight items add up to £11.11.

Aldi, Tesco, Morrisons and M&S had not published their 2026 Christmas dinner prices when this article was written on 8 November. Last year most of them announced in December.

For comparison, here is what each offered in 2025. These are last year's prices, not this year's.

Aldi cut the price of its 2025 dinner for six to £9.31 on 4 December, using the same eight-item list. The turkey was £7.35 and its Super Six vegetables were 5p each. For a family of four that was about £2.33 a head.

Tesco's 2025 dinner for six cost £9.55, but only with a Clubcard. The 3kg turkey was £7.50 with the card, half its usual £5 per kg, and the four vegetables were 15p each. It was sold in most large Tesco stores from 19 December.

Morrisons did not publish a full dinner bundle in 2025. More Card holders could buy carrots, parsnips, sprouts and a swede for 5p each from 18 to 26 December, and 1.5kg of roasting potatoes was £1 for all shoppers.

M&S did not offer a comparable value Christmas dinner, so Rochdale Daily could not price the same basket there.

On last year's prices, Aldi was cheapest without any loyalty card, Tesco came close only for Clubcard holders, and Lidl's opening 2026 price sits £1.80 above Aldi's final 2025 figure.

Loyalty schemes made a real difference in 2025. Tesco's turkey price halved with a Clubcard, and Morrisons' 5p vegetables needed a More Card. Both cards are free to sign up for.

Reduced "yellow sticker" food can also cut the bill. Which? found that Tesco and Morrisons have no set reduction times.

Aldi told Which? that reductions vary by store but are likely near closing time, with fresh food cut by 30% or 75% on its last day. Lidl staff usually reduce items first thing in the morning and a few hours before closing, while M&S reductions are also likely near closing.

Fresh Christmas vegetables and turkeys that reach their date on Christmas Eve are often reduced, but stock is not guaranteed and shoppers relying on it risk going without.

Rochdale Daily will update this comparison as Aldi, Tesco, Morrisons and M&S announce their 2026 prices.

Source: Lidl prices via Yahoo News UK and BritBrief; Aldi press office; The Grocer; Morrisons press office; Which?.

articles.title: Plans approved for 21 new apartments in former office block in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: St James Place on Yorkshire Street will be transformed into residential apartments after sitting empty for eight years, with planning permission granted for the redevelopment.
articles.content_html:
A former office block in Rochdale will be converted into 21 new apartments after sitting empty for nearly a decade.

St James Place, located on Yorkshire Street, has received planning permission from Rochdale Council for the redevelopment, which aims to provide much-needed housing in the area.

Developer Alam Investments plans to create a mix of one and two-bedroom flats, each featuring its own living, dining, and kitchen space. The project is described as a 'sensitive and appropriate reuse of the building', with only internal changes planned to the structure.

A heritage statement was required for the application due to the proximity of the Grade II-listed St Mary’s Ukrainian Catholic Church.

The planning documents noted that the building has been vacant for approximately eight years and is in need of investment and reuse, stating that the proposed scheme will contribute positively to the vitality and regeneration of Rochdale town centre.

This redevelopment is seen as a significant step towards addressing the housing shortage in the area, providing residents with modern living spaces in a sustainable location.

articles.title: Boyes opens new store in Middleton Shopping Centre tomorrow
articles.excerpt: Discount chain Boyes will open its new store in Middleton Shopping Centre, filling the gap left by Wilko's closure.
articles.content_html:
Discount chain Boyes is set to open its new store in Middleton Shopping Centre tomorrow, 6 November, at 9am. This new store will occupy the former Wilko site, which closed earlier this year, leaving a gap in the local retail landscape.

For the past few weeks, contractors and staff have been preparing the two-floor space to welcome customers. Boyes aims to provide a wide range of products, including everyday essentials, electrical items, DIY supplies, fashion, footwear, craft and hobby materials, homewares, and seasonal goods.

Local residents have expressed enthusiasm about the new store. Yvonne Marie Knott stated, "Boyes has everything you need in a store," while Sharon Dyson added, "Can’t wait, Middleton needs this."

Kathleen Hall also shared her excitement, saying, "Looking forward to it!"

The opening of Boyes is expected to bring a boost to the local economy and provide residents with a convenient shopping option. As the store prepares to welcome its first customers, it will help fill the retail void left by Wilko's closure.

articles.title: Former non-league footballer James Moore builds multi-million pound shop empire
articles.excerpt: James Moore, a former non-league footballer, has established a successful retail business, Mintro, with eight stores across the North West, including Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
James Moore, a former non-league footballer, has transitioned from the pitch to the retail world, building a multi-million pound business empire with his company Mintro.

The 38-year-old, who played for clubs including Bury FC and Glossop North End, now operates eight stores across the North West, including one in Rochdale.

Moore's journey began at the age of 18 when he took a Saturday job at BrightHouse in Hyde.

His success in retail led him to manage various stores, eventually taking on a Cash Generator shop in Rochdale in 2017, which he transformed into his own brand, Mintro.

The store focuses on buying and selling pre-owned technology, jewellery, and designer items without the pawn shop model of loans and interest.

Despite the challenges posed by the Covid pandemic, which temporarily closed his stores, Moore leveraged the situation to secure financing for expansion.

His business now generates around £5 million annually, with plans to grow further, including a recent sponsorship deal with Stockport County FC, a team he once played against as a child.

Moore's story showcases resilience and adaptability, demonstrating how skills from sports can translate into business success.
articles.social_headline: James Moore turns former football career into a thriving retail empire in Rochdale.

Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter ‌ Dad-of-two James, now aged 38, is the founder of Mintro, which buys and sells pre-owned phones and technology, jewellery, watches and designer handbags, and which now has eight stores across the North West, including five in Greater Manchester. He has done so alongside a fruitful football career which has seen him play for a number of local non-league sides, most notably Bury FC. View 4 Images James outside one of his eight stores Central defender James played in front of thousands of fans at the Shakers' Gigg Lane, alongside spells at Glossop North End, Atherton Collieries, Cheadle Town, Abbey Hey and Trafford FC. ‌ He has now hung up his boots with his business turning over in the region of £5 million per year, and plans afoot to take it national. James says he cut his teeth on the shop floor. His job at BrightHouse saw him promoted to manager, and he spent time in London running a store there. "I won a number of accolades and realised I wasn't too bad at this retail game" he told the Manchester Evening News. "I was capable of speaking to the CEO in the same way as an entry-level member of staff," he said. He said he soon became homesick and returned to Greater Manchester where, aged 21, a friend of his dad's helped get him a job at the then Cash Generator store on Oldham Street in the Northern Quarter . "I was just pretty good at it," he said. View 4 Images James cut his teeth on the shop floor of BrightHouse and Cash Generator ‌ He went on to run the brand's shops in Hyde and Wythenshawe before being headhunted by a franchisee to run a branch in Harpurhey , who then went on to acquire several more. That relationship ended and, at age 30, James found himself unemployed. However, in 2017, a franchisee offered him the chance to take on a Cash Generator shop in Rochdale that would otherwise likely have closed down, at just 'stock costs.' Having always worked for other people, that, he said, was his 'foot in the door' that allowed him to start to build his own business. He said he 'panicked' when the Covid pandemic saw stores shut, but that it turned out to be a blessing in disguise, as it allowed him to access finance in order to grow the business. ‌ He took on another store at Salford Precinct and opened new ones on Princes Street in his hometown of Stockport, on Newport Street in Bolton , and in Huddersfield and Bradford in West Yorkshire. He also now has stores on Piccadilly in central Manchester and in Blackpool. View 4 Images James said there was a 'lot of negativity' around pre-owned stores but insisted they provide a vital service In September this year, he said he decided he wanted to 'go in a different direction' and brought the stores into his own Mintro brand. They have since announced a sponsorship deal with Stockport County FC. "It was quite a poignant one, as I'd gone from scoring goals at Edgeley Park as a kid to sponsoring them," he said. Mintro stores are not pawn shops, as there are no loans and no interest accrues. Instead, they will buy items outright for a cash price agreed with the customer. They then have the option to buy it back within 28 days, plus a storage fee of 15-35 percent, before it can be sold to other customers. ‌ James said that the 'pre-owned market' is 'tarnished a bit' and 'has a lot of negativity around it' but insisted they offer a vital service for people in a variety of situations and that they 'always offered a fair price.' "Everyone has bought and sold on eBay, everyone has bought and sold on Vinted, it's the same thing really," he said. He said they offered a two-year guarantee on products and said they 'worked closely with the police' and had stringent processes to prevent the sale of stolen goods to them. James, who has two daughters aged 15 and seven, and who now lives in Lytham in Lancs, said he did not want to 'stand still' and has plans to expand further, with his dream to make Mintro a nationwide household name. "I'm definitely proud, but there is still a lot more in the tank, and a bigger business to be built," he said. articles.title: EG On The Move plans to rebuild Rochdale forecourt
articles.excerpt: EG On The Move has announced plans for a significant redevelopment of a filling station in Rochdale, aiming to enhance its services and facilities.
articles.content_html:
EG On The Move has unveiled plans to demolish and rebuild a filling station located on the A58 in Rochdale, Greater Manchester. This initiative is part of the company's ongoing growth strategy, which aims to modernise its facilities and improve customer service.

The proposed redevelopment will involve a complete knock-down of the existing structure, followed by the construction of a new forecourt. This project is expected to enhance the overall customer experience at the site.

The plans are currently under review, and further details regarding the timeline for the project have yet to be announced. Local residents and businesses may be affected during the construction phase, but the company aims to minimise disruption.

As the project progresses, updates will be provided to keep the community informed.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council awards contract for Empty Homes Leasing Programme
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to CAREPOINT HC LIMITED for the GM Empty Homes TA Leasing Programme, aimed at providing temporary accommodation for families.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to CAREPOINT HC LIMITED for the GM Empty Homes Temporary Accommodation (TA) Leasing Programme. This framework contract is set for an initial term of four years or until the contract value reaches £3.5 million, whichever comes first.

The programme aims to lease or acquire 2-4 bedroom homes to provide temporary accommodation for families that the Council has a duty to support under sections 188, 190, or 193 of the Housing Act.

The initiative seeks to incentivise property owners with homes that have been empty for six months or more to bring them back into use, thereby reducing the costs associated with temporary accommodation.

In addition to the framework contract, a call-off contract has also been awarded to CAREPOINT HC LIMITED for a minimum of 20 to a maximum of 32 properties. The value of this call-off contract is not guaranteed, reflecting the flexible nature of the agreement.

This initiative is significant for Rochdale as it addresses the pressing need for safe and secure accommodation for families facing housing challenges. By utilising empty homes, the Council aims to improve housing availability while managing costs effectively.
articles.social_headline: Rochdale Council partners with CAREPOINT HC for Empty Homes Leasing Programme

articles.title: Zambrero to give away free burritos at new Mellor Street restaurant in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Zambrero will hand out hundreds of free burritos and bowls from 11am to 2pm on Thursday 12 November to mark its new Mellor Street restaurant, which opened in September.
articles.content_html:
Zambrero is giving away free burritos and bowls at its new Mellor Street restaurant in Rochdale next week, as a thank-you to the town six weeks after it opened.

The Free Burrito Day takes place on Thursday 12 November, from 11am to 2pm. The company says it will hand out hundreds of freshly made burritos and bowls during the three-hour window, and is advising people to arrive early to avoid the queues. Zambrero's resident scratch DJ, NC, will be playing hip hop and crowd favourites throughout.

The restaurant opened on 25 September and is Zambrero's first site in Rochdale. It offers dine-in, takeaway and delivery, has seating for 18, and is close to the town centre and local colleges. According to the company, the opening has created six jobs.

The menu centres on burritos and bowls, alongside tacos, nachos and quesadillas, made to order at the counter. Customers can choose from slow-cooked fillings, salad, rice, beans and toppings, and there are vegetarian, vegan and halal options.

The site also brings the chain's Plate 4 Plate scheme to Rochdale, under which a meal is donated to someone in need for every burrito or bowl bought. Zambrero says the scheme has provided more than 110 million meals worldwide.

Damian Bennett, Zambrero's development agent for Greater Manchester and West Yorkshire, said: "We've had a fantastic response since opening our doors in Rochdale and this Free Burrito Day is our way of thanking the local community for its support. We can't wait to welcome residents, students and local workers to come along, enjoy a free burrito or bowl and experience what Zambrero is all about."

He added that every burrito and bowl given away on the day, and bought afterwards, would count towards the Plate 4 Plate programme.

Rochdale is Zambrero's 18th UK opening since the brand arrived in Britain in 2021, with other sites in London, Manchester, Birmingham, Reading, Essex, Basingstoke, Northampton and Glasgow. The company was founded in Australia in 2005 and now has more than 350 locations worldwide.

For town-centre businesses, a new food outlet within reach of the colleges adds to the lunchtime trade around Mellor Street.

Source: press release from Zambrero supplied to Rochdale Daily. Photograph: Zambrero / supplied.

articles.title: Sandbrook Way KFC licence now permits late-night service until 5am
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's public licensing register shows updated permission for late-night refreshment at the Sandbrook Way KFC, with the restaurant area due to close at midnight under a licence condition.
articles.content_html:
The KFC at Sandbrook Way, Edinburgh Way, Rochdale, has a premises licence permitting late-night refreshment until 5am on every day of the week, according to Rochdale Borough Council's public licensing register.

The register identifies the premises as KFC, OL11 1RY, and names Chicken Cabins Ltd trading as KFC as the licence holder. It lists licence PL(N)1021 with an effective date of 17 October 2026. The permitted premises hours are shown as 10am to 5am, while late-night refreshment is authorised from 11pm to 5am, indoors and outdoors.

There is an important distinction between the permission and what customers can expect on any particular night. The licence sets out what is legally authorised; it is not a verified announcement that every service is operating throughout those hours. A condition in the published record says the restaurant area is to close at midnight, with delivery and drive-through service afterwards.

An earlier version of the same council record, viewed as at 11 October 2026, listed midnight closing on most days and 1am on Friday and Saturday. The updated register therefore records a materially later authorised finish time. It does not explain the commercial reasons for the change or give a launch date for extended service.

The licence includes conditions covering CCTV, door supervision during late-night licensing hours, management of noise and litter, and requests for customers to leave quietly. These are licence requirements, not evidence of a specific incident at the premises.

Customers wanting to know whether collection, drive-through or delivery is currently available after midnight should check directly with the restaurant. Rochdale Daily will update this report if the operator confirms its actual trading timetable.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council awards contract for family temporary accommodation services
articles.excerpt: The Bond Board Limited has been awarded a contract to manage the Homeless Family Leasing Scheme, providing vital support to homeless families in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract for the management and support services of the Homeless Family Leasing Scheme (HFLS) to The Bond Board Limited. This initiative aims to provide essential tenancy management and support for homeless families placed in temporary accommodation.

The HFLS will oversee approximately 40 leased properties, offering services that include property management, tenancy sustainment, and move-on support. This contract is part of the council's ongoing efforts to address homelessness in the area and provide stable housing solutions for families in need.

In addition to the HFLS contract, the council has also awarded a separate contract for the A Bed for Every Night (ABEN) Dispersed Accommodation and Support Services to Stepping Stone Projects.

This service will provide around 34 units of accommodation for homeless individuals and those at risk of rough sleeping, along with housing-related support to help them achieve stable living conditions.

These contracts are significant steps in tackling homelessness in Rochdale, reflecting the council's commitment to supporting vulnerable families and individuals. The Bond Board Limited and Stepping Stone Projects are expected to begin their services shortly, contributing to the local community's efforts to reduce homelessness.

articles.title: Rochdale's Atom Valley project aims to create thousands of jobs and homes
articles.excerpt: The Atom Valley development aims to create 17 million square feet of employment space and 7,000 new homes in Rochdale, with the first phase already underway.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale is set to undergo a significant transformation with the announcement of the Atom Valley development, which aims to create 17 million square feet of employment space and 7,000 new homes.

This ambitious project is expected to generate around 20,000 highly skilled jobs in the technology and manufacturing sectors, addressing the town's long-standing issues of low wages and lost investment.

The development is spearheaded by the Rochdale Development Agency, led by managing director Rachel Laver, who emphasised the importance of making local residents aware of the opportunities that Atom Valley will bring.

Laver stated, "I want to do more of bringing what we do closer to people," highlighting the need for community engagement in the project.

The first milestone of the Atom Valley initiative was the completion of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park, which is now equipped to attract international businesses.

This centre is seen as a crucial step towards revitalising the local economy and changing perceptions about job opportunities in Rochdale.

As the project progresses, local residents and businesses are encouraged to engage with the developments.

The RDA aims to ensure that the benefits of Atom Valley are felt by the community, fostering growth and reducing the need for residents to seek employment opportunities outside of Rochdale.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The multi-billion plan to transform Rochdale - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news The multi-billion plan to transform Rochdale Boasting stunning Pennine views and 20-minute train links to Manchester, Rochdale has long struggled with low wages and lost investment. Sitting down with the M.E.N., development boss Rachel Laver outlines how Atom Valley and station linear parks will finally make the town's wealth stay put. View 8 Images Rochdale town centre. (Image: Rochdale Council) Add to preferred sources Comments News George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter 16:59, 01 Nov 2026 Updated 12:12, 02 Nov 2026 Rochdale has trams, trains, motorway links as well as stunning views of the Pennines and a rich cultural and historic heritage. It has everything you’d expect of an area with the ability to thrive, so why it has lower than average salaries and high deprivation is a puzzling question. But things are changing in the north-eastern borough of Greater Manchester. The civic centre, Rochdale town centre, has already undergone a major facelift. Yet there is more to come for the town, with plans to link up the town to its train station. To get the very latest from Manchester's political scene in your newsfeed - click here to add the MEN as your preferred Google source ‌ The Atom Valley development zone is on the way, which is estimated to bring 17m sq ft employment space, 7,000 new homes and offer 20,000 ‘highly skilled’ roles in the technology and manufacturing sectors. The first tangible milestone of Atom Valley arrived earlier this month when the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) was completed in the Northern Gateway part of the project. It now stands proud at Kingsway Business Park, ready to be kitted out with all the technology needed to house international innovative businesses and manufacturers. View 8 Images Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale where ground was broken on new Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre (Image: Sean Hansford | Manchester Evening News) Atom Valley was even described by Prime Minister Andy Burnham as the start of a ‘new decade of growth’ in Greater Manchester during his days as the city-region’s mayor. ‌ But many won’t have heard of the organisation behind a majority of these major projects - Rochdale Development Agency. It is a reasonable assumption to say the RDA are the construction arm of Rochdale council because if there is a council-led building project, it’s likely to be the RDA delivering it. However, the RDA’s recently appointed managing director, Rachel Laver, said there are many more strings to their bow - or perhaps more accurately, more excavators to their diggers. Rachel sat down with the Manchester Evening News and divulged her lofty ambitions for Rochdale. View 8 Images Rachel Laver, managing director of the Rochdale Development Agency (Image: RDA) ‌ The popular misquote of ‘build it and they will come’ from the 1989 film Field of Dreams has become part of common vernacular. In a nutshell, that is exactly how the RDA boss feels about the future of Rochdale. Rachel said: “I want to do more of bringing what we do closer to people. We talk about Northern Gateway and Atom Valley, a huge initiative bigger than Trafford Park and a collaboration between Bury , Oldham and Rochdale councils. “But I want local people to know it’s for them, not just some nebulous thing you hear people talking about. “I think we need to bring Northern Gateway and Atom Valley closer to the people of Rochdale so they can see there are job opportunities there. ‌ “We want businesses to come to Rochdale but we want businesses in Rochdale to grow.” Don't let an algorithm decide what Manchester news you see - click here to add the MEN as your preferred Google source The RDA boss felt her job was to work with businesses and organisations to create opportunity. She explained there is this feeling that if you want to be successful, you have to leave Rochdale. Atom Valley is one of the big projects that she hopes can change that mindset by providing high skilled jobs locally - and lots of them. But she highlighted there are some manufacturers in the area already doing that, such as Heatsense Cables making parts for space rockets and Hutchinson Engineering who make parts for JCB and Caterpillar. ‌ “You listen to the press and you’d think manufacturing is dead, it’s not,” said Rachel. “Manufacturers are doing amazingly well. “Rochdale has a manufacturing history and we still have those ties.” She wants to see greater space and funding to provide growth for businesses. Rachel explained that funding pots often go for the ‘low hanging fruit’ and give it to the big cities. That is a big downfall for Rochdale in her eyes - that it’s not a city centre like Manchester. “Quite often the funding goes into the main centres and the areas on the periphery don’t get as much investment,” Rachel added. “So I think we need to bang the drum to make sure we get our fair share.” ‌ View 8 Images Baillie Street in Rochdale town centre (Image: Sean Hansford | Manchester Evening News) According to her data, ‘£10 goes around the economy two times in Rochdale’, compared to a well-functioning economy where it goes around seven times. This means that if a project is started, the contract for that job may go to a company outside the area and employ other people from outside the area - and the money goes with them to benefit another local economy. So making the £10 go around the economy more times would mean more local businesses winning contracts, employing local people and providing more apprenticeships and training for young people. With more and more young people not in education, employment, or training (NEETs), Rachel explained pushing for more apprenticeships and training is vital for upskilling the next generation in Rochdale. ‌ Focusing on getting the ‘£10 around more times’ is something she believes will help boost the local economy in the long run. But in order to attract outside investment into Atom Valley, Rochdale needs a ‘whole package’, Rachel adds. This is why there is a plan for thousands of new homes to be built around Atom Valley and why the RDA is lobbying with Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) to increase tram regularity, new bus timetables and improve the road network. View 8 Images The new Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale (Image: RDA) There is already work happening on the Simister Island upgrade, coming in 2029 and in 2023, getting the Queen Elizabeth II Way extension off Junction 19 in South Heywood has proved vital for access to businesses in that area. ‌ Rachel said that affordable housing is important and understands why, politically, it is a big thing to deliver. But she says ‘aspirational housing’ is also needed to attract the high-earning clientele that would come with the Atom Valley project. She believes there is so much the borough could offer for executive homes - views of the Pennines, wonderful greenery and brilliant transport connections to Yorkshire and Manchester city centre . It takes less than 20 minutes to get to Manchester Victoria by train. The RDA boss went onto how they are helping to deliver this ‘full package’ - through making the town centre more vibrant and, simply, a nicer place to be. They are already taking action on this by starting on a housing project right next to Rochdale station. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place , in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. ‌ It will be followed by a revamp of the station, including a new project called ‘Station Platform Gardens’, which will bring life and greenery back to the disused platform. Currently there are just ‘steps that go to nowhere’ at the station, Rachel explained. View 8 Images The former Central Retail Park site development under construction (Image: Rochdale council) She continued: “At the moment I think the station feels really disconnected from the town centre. As you go down Drake Street it isn’t very welcoming. “As we build up John Rennie Place, it’s going to get so much more footfall, which uplifts the area. Then people invest when you’ve got the footfall as well. ‌ “Excitingly and innovatively, we’re leading on a project called Station Platform Gardens. There is a redundant station platform at Rochdale, so we’re going to create a linear park. “That will have healthy walks. But on the other side of the station, the park and ride will be turned into a multi-storey car park and that whole area will be redeveloped.” The area in front of the station will eventually be shut off to traffic and have a plaza there - ‘a whole different feel’. Rachel adds that ‘it will be a much better welcome to Rochdale’ a true gateway you’d expect when arriving by train. Another role the RDA plays is in culture and heritage - running around 54 programmes across the borough. ‌ RDA also operates Grade-I listed Rochdale Town Hall and the Touchstones museum and art gallery across the Esplanade. Touchstones will be reopened in Spring 2027, Rachel revealed. View 8 Images Rochdale Town Hall (Image: Rochdale Council) But it isn’t just Rochdale getting all the love, the outside towns are all seeing big projects coming forward. In Middleton, there is the Mayoral Development Corporation (MDC) moving forwards . This will see the council buying out Warwick Mill so it can finally be redeveloped. Rachel said there had been some costly realisations when it came to the abandoned spinning mill - with around 1,500 tyres found dumped there. ‌ The cost of properly disposing of tyres is most likely the reason for this fly-tipping, but it’s now a cost the local authority will have to bear once it finalises the deal to take over the site later this year. Outside of that, the RDA will also be helping support the delivery of the MDC, which aims to bring Metrolink trams to Middleton ; create new homes on brownfield plots; build high-quality business premises; and better public areas, roads and pathways. View 8 Images Warwick Mill in Middleton (Image: Rochdale council) When asked how Rochdale will look in 10 years time, Rachel said: “I would like to say we’d see thriving communities. But we should see more town centres living across the whole of the borough, not just Rochdale. ‌ “The borough as a whole has the capacity to take a lot of housing. We know the government has set very high housing targets and Manchester city centre is struggling for space. “We can take the housing. So 7,000 new homes are proposed in Atom Valley and I think all that investment will support the local economy. We will get £10 going around the economy far more. “I’m really excited about the SMMC and Atom Valley and the types of businesses we could have here. It is creating that cluster which will give us strength and opportunities that people don’t need to move away from Rochdale. “We want young people in Rochdale to aspire to be the best, but we want them to come back. ‌ “We want people to be proud of Rochdale and shouting and saying ‘come, because it’s great’. Because it genuinely is. “I think it will look different in 10 years time. We’ll have better connectivity, better skilled people and higher value jobs.” GET MORE FROM US Choose Manchester Evening News as a 'Preferred Source' on Google News for quick access to the news you value. articles.title: Heywood’s Little Play Town put up for sale as owner reassures families it will stay open
articles.excerpt: Owner Jackie is seeking a buyer after four years, with Little Play Town remaining open and existing party bookings going ahead as planned.
articles.content_html:
Little Play Town in Heywood has been put up for sale, with owner Jackie reassuring families that the children’s role play business will remain open and existing party bookings will go ahead as planned.

Announcing the decision, Jackie said she was selling for personal reasons after four years of building the business alongside her team.

“This is something I never thought I’d be writing, and it’s been an incredibly difficult decision to make,” she said.

Jackie described Little Play Town as her “pride and joy” and thanked the staff, customers and families who have supported it.

She stressed that the sale announcement does not mean the venue is closing. Sessions will continue as normal, and families with parties booked do not need to change their plans.

The search is now on for a new owner to take over the established leasehold business. Jackie said a support package lasting up to three months would be available to help the buyer settle in.

The announcement highlights the existing staff team, supportive customer base and opportunities to introduce additional themed events, sessions and experiences. Jackie also described the landlord as proactive and supportive.

She hopes to find someone who will build on the business’s first four years and continue providing a place for children to play and make memories.

Anyone interested in buying Little Play Town can register their interest by emailing info@littleplaytownheywood.co.uk.

For local families, the immediate message is that the venue remains open and booked celebrations will continue as planned.

articles.title: Middleton designated as mayoral development area to boost regeneration
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig has designated Middleton as a mayoral development area, aiming to enhance economic development and housing in the town.
articles.content_html:
Middleton has been officially designated as a mayoral development area by Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig, marking a significant step forward in the town's regeneration efforts.

This decision follows a six-week public consultation and was approved by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) last month, with Rochdale Council also endorsing the proposal.

The establishment of the Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation is expected to accelerate economic development and regeneration in the area. The GMCA highlighted that this designation presents a substantial opportunity to improve Middleton town centre and its surrounding communities.

The new development corporation aims to attract both public and private investment, facilitating the construction of approximately 1,500 new homes, including affordable housing. This initiative is part of a broader strategy to enhance the living conditions and economic prospects for local residents.

The Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government has been notified of this designation, which will be formalised by an official order.

articles.title: New industrial units planned at Caldershaw Business Centre in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Nine new industrial units are set to be built at Caldershaw Business Centre, aiming to boost local employment and support entrepreneurs.
articles.content_html:
Nine new industrial units are planned for construction at the Caldershaw Business Centre in Rochdale. The initiative aims to create jobs and provide opportunities for local entrepreneurs, according to a proposal submitted to Rochdale Council by Adil Iqbal of IQ7 Ltd.

The new units will occupy a previously disused area of land adjacent to Unit 6/5d at the business centre, which is located off Rooley Moor Road. The site, currently overgrown and littered, previously housed a mill building that has since been demolished.

The development is expected to transform this neglected space into a productive environment for new businesses.

Each of the nine units will range in size from 84 square metres to 164 square metres, featuring roller shutter doors, pedestrian access, small office spaces, and WC facilities.

The total industrial floor space will be approximately 1,170 square metres, providing a significant boost to local business infrastructure and potentially attracting new enterprises to the area.

The planning application is currently under review, with further updates anticipated as the project progresses. This development is significant as it aims to stimulate local entrepreneurship and job creation in Rochdale, addressing the need for more business space in the community.

articles.title: Construction milestone reached for Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: The Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park has completed its base build, marking a significant step in the development of Rochdale's advanced materials hub.
articles.content_html:
The Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale has reached a major milestone with the completion of its base build.

This development is part of the Atom Valley Innovation District, which aims to foster advanced materials and manufacturing innovation in the region.

Designed by Bond Bryan, the 30,000 sq. ft centre will serve as a vital link between research, specialist facilities, and commercial production.

It is expected to generate £107 million in economic value over the next decade, supporting the transition of new technologies from concept to commercial application.

The Rochdale Development Agency (RDA) has spearheaded the project in collaboration with the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), The University of Manchester, and other innovation partners. The next phase will focus on the fit-out of the centre, with operations anticipated to commence in 2027.

Mark Adey, director at Bond Bryan, highlighted the importance of creating environments that facilitate innovation and commercialisation. The SMMC is designed to adapt to emerging technologies and business needs, ensuring it remains relevant as industries evolve.

articles.title: Rochdale’s Deckers Hospitality Group acquires historic drinks wholesaler Tate-Smith
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale-based family group has bought the Malton drinks wholesaler, with existing staff staying and Harry Tate-Smith continuing as trading director.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale-based Deckers Hospitality Group has acquired North Yorkshire drinks wholesaler Tate-Smith, adding a business founded in 1888 to its portfolio.

The deal brings together two family businesses. Deckers is led by siblings Max Brierley and Victoria Cosgrove and operates in hospitality, wholesale and e-commerce.

Tate-Smith, based in Malton, supplies soft and alcoholic drinks across North Yorkshire. The business had been owned by the same family for six generations.

According to the announcement issued on 22 October, it will continue trading as Tate-Smith Ltd. All current staff will remain, and Harry Tate-Smith will continue in the business as trading director.

Paul and Cate Tate-Smith sold the company. Paul said the time was right to pass it to a business that could support its next stage, while retaining a role for their son.

Maxwell Brierley, of Deckers Hospitality Group, said: “Like us Tate-Smith is a family-run business with an impressive history. We felt it was the perfect fit for us as we continue to develop and grow our portfolio, and we welcome them to our family.”

For Rochdale, the acquisition marks an expansion of a locally based group into an established Yorkshire wholesale business. The release does not disclose a purchase price or announce any additional Rochdale jobs.

AAB and Schofield Sweeney advised Tate-Smith’s shareholders. Deckers was advised by Pannone Corporate and Cowgills, part of the Sumer Group.

articles.title: Rochdale Council awards contract for Queen's Park SEND improvement project
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to enhance the play area at Queen's Park, Heywood, focusing on inclusivity for children with special educational needs.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to MASSEY & HARRIS (ENGINEERING) LIMITED for the Queen's Park SEND and Improvement Project. This initiative aims to create a more inclusive play area at Queen's Park in Heywood, enhancing facilities for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The project will involve several key improvements, including the extension of the existing play area, the installation of a dance arch, the creation of a sensory area surrounding the dance arch, and the addition of a wheelchair swing.

These enhancements are designed to ensure that all children can enjoy the park's facilities, regardless of their physical abilities.

The decision to improve the play area reflects the council's commitment to inclusivity and accessibility in public spaces. By investing in these facilities, Rochdale Council aims to provide a safe and engaging environment for all children in the community, promoting social interaction and play.

The next steps will involve the commencement of construction works, with further updates expected as the project progresses. This development is significant for local families, particularly those with children who have SEND, as it will provide them with improved recreational opportunities in their community.

articles.title: New Domino's Pizza branch opens on Manchester Road in Middleton
articles.excerpt: A new Domino's Pizza branch has opened on Manchester Road in Middleton, generating mixed reactions from the local community, with some welcoming the addition while others express concerns about local businesses and traffic.
articles.content_html:
A new Domino's Pizza branch has opened on Manchester Road in Middleton, generating mixed reactions from local residents. Some are excited about the convenience of having a pizza outlet nearby, while others have raised concerns about its impact on local businesses.

Local shop owners fear that the new competition could affect their sales and foot traffic. The branch aims to provide quick meal options for families and individuals in the area.

Local councillors are discussing the implications of the new branch, particularly regarding traffic management and support for existing businesses. They want to ensure that the new outlet does not disrupt the local economy.

As opinions remain divided, it will be important for the community to monitor how the new Domino's integrates into Middleton and what measures are taken to address residents' concerns.

articles.title: Remembrance Sunday services planned across Rochdale borough
articles.excerpt: Residents will gather on November 8 to honour those who served in the armed forces, with parades and services in multiple towns.
articles.content_html:
Residents across the Rochdale borough are set to come together on Sunday, November 8, to pay their respects to those who have made sacrifices defending the country. Remembrance Day commemorations will feature a series of services and parades in towns including Rochdale, Castleton, Heywood, Littleborough, Middleton, Milnrow, Norden, and Wardle.

The events will see representatives from the Navy, Army, and Royal Air Force join veterans and civic dignitaries. Each service will include hymns, prayers, the Last Post, a two-minute silence, and the national anthem, ensuring a solemn tribute to those who served.

In Heywood, the parade will commence at 10.15am on Tower Street, proceeding to St James’ Street before arriving at Heywood Memorial Gardens for a service at 10.55am.

Similarly, in Middleton, the parade will gather at 10.10am facing the Harbord Harbord pub, departing for Middleton Remembrance Gardens at 10.20am, with the service starting at 10.45am.

In Rochdale, participants will assemble outside The Flying Horse Hotel in Packer Street at 10.30am, where they will be joined by ward councillors and other civic guests.

The parade will march to the Cenotaph for the service at 10.55am, followed by a march past before returning to The Flying Horse Hotel.

articles.title: Rochdale station regeneration scheme progresses with new homes and public square
articles.excerpt: A significant regeneration project around Rochdale railway station is underway, featuring new homes and a public square, aimed at improving access to the town centre.
articles.content_html:
A regeneration scheme aimed at transforming the area around Rochdale railway station is making significant strides, according to local officials.

The project includes the construction of 81 new homes on vacant land adjacent to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park, part of a broader initiative to enhance connectivity between the train station and the town centre.

The development, named John Rennie Place in honour of the Scottish civil engineer who designed the Rochdale Canal, began in November 2026 and is expected to be completed by December 2027. The homes will consist of two, three, and four-bedroom properties and are being built as affordable net zero homes, marking a significant step in sustainable housing for the area.

In addition to the residential units, the regeneration plan includes the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 apartments on a brownfield site at the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road.

This initiative is part of a larger effort to reconnect the station, which historically served as a hub for industrial transport, with the town centre, reflecting the changing needs of the community.

The project was made possible by a successful bid for £15 million from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund, which has enabled the local authority to move forward after years of planning and investment challenges.

The local council reports that the development is already benefiting the local economy and community, providing much-needed housing and improving public spaces.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The scheme to regenerate land around Rochdale station progressing | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The scheme to regenerate land around Rochdale station progressing George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 24, 2026 | 9:23 AM Print A scheme which would transform the gateway into Rochdale is making significant progress, town hall bosses say. Some 81 two, three-and four-bedroom homes are currently under construction on vacant land next to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park. This forms part of a wider scheme to create a connection between the train station and the town centre. The wider regeneration of the area around Rochdale railway station also involves the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 new apartments on a brownfield site on the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. The train station in Rochdale was once a hub for industrial business generations ago, so the distance between the station and the town centre was purposeful separation. But as times changed, society changed and the station suddenly started transporting people, not goods. This is why there is an idea to improve access and avenues from the station and the main hub of the town. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place, in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. The project, approved years ago, was unlocked following a successful bid for £15m from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund. The transformation has been on the cards for a long time, but the local authority struggled to get the investment until last year. The properties will be the first affordable net zero homes delivered as part of a housing scheme supported by the council. The local authority says the development is already delivering benefits to the local economy and community. Contractor Willmott Dixon, working on behalf of the council, has already spent £3.3m with local civil engineering firm, Hovington Ltd, and supported a total of 95 weeks of apprenticeship and T-Level training, including three T-Level placements from Hopwood Hall College. Seven local people are also employed on the project, including two people who were previously unemployed, with the council’s work and skills team supporting the recruitment. Tommy Patterson, 22, from Middleton, is one of the local people working on the new homes. He said: “I had been out of work for six months when the job centre arranged for me to get my CSCS card and that led to me securing a scaffolding apprenticeship here on site. I have always worked and had been let go, so getting this job was a lifeline. “I live on my own and I was struggling to pay my bills. It’s great to work here. Everyone is lovely; it’s a smashing team.” Daniel Fletcher, 17, is studying for a T Level in design, surveying and planning at Hopwood Hall College, said: “I really like it here. I’ve been talking to the different trades delivering this project, so I’ve been exposed to different parts of the job, and I have the freedom to go onto site on my own. It’s already changed massively since I started in the summer.” The project is being led by Rochdale Development Agency (RDA) on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council. Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for housing and regeneration at Rochdale Borough Council, said: ”We want local people and businesses to feel the benefit of local projects and it’s great to see that these benefits are already being felt on this development before a single house has even been completed. “By ensuring that social value is embedded in our procurement system, we’re making sure that local people are invested in the extensive regeneration which is taking place on their doorstep and are benefitting from the economic transformation we’re spearheading across the borough. That’s how it should be and how it will continue to be.” Work to create 142 apartments next to the new homes is ongoing, with the procurement of a delivery partner expected to get underway soon. articles.title: Community efforts revive historic Lodge Mill after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: Lodge Mill in Middleton, a historic site dating back to 1850, is seeing a revival thanks to community support following a fire that left it in ruins.
articles.content_html:
Lodge Mill, one of the oldest mills in Middleton, is undergoing a revival after a devastating fire left the historic structure nearly destroyed. The fire, which occurred earlier this year, resulted in the loss of significant parts of the mill, including a children's dance studio and an ice cream parlour. Fortunately, no injuries were reported during the incident.

The mill, which dates back to around 1850, was deemed uninsurable following the fire, complicating efforts for its restoration. However, local residents and volunteers have rallied together to support the rebuilding efforts.

A GoFundMe page was established, raising over £7,000 to aid in the restoration process, demonstrating the community's commitment to preserving this historic landmark.

Martin and Paula, who were actively working on renovating the three floors above Lodge Mill prior to the fire, are now at the forefront of the recovery efforts.

Thanks to the dedication of volunteers, life is returning to Lodge Mill, with plans to restore it to its former glory.

The revival of Lodge Mill is significant not only for its historical value but also for the community spirit it embodies.

As restoration efforts continue, the mill is set to become a focal point for local activities once again, highlighting the importance of community involvement in preserving local heritage.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The potential return of Lodge Mill | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The potential return of Lodge Mill George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 24, 2026 | 2 hours ago Print Community effort to clear up rubble at Lodge Mill in Middleton Lodge Mill in Middleton was devastated by a fire six months ago. Now there is hope for its future thanks to some dedicated business owners, volunteers and one avid ice cream fan. In March, firefighters were called to the massive blaze that left businesses in tatters and left the historic mill a shell. Several businesses were based on the ground floor of the building, believed to be one of the oldest mills in Middleton. A children’s dance studio, an ice cream parlour, a tea room, a dog chiropractor business and the Engine House event space, which held weddings, functions and parties, were all lost in the fire. The former silk and cotton mill, on Townley Street, dates back to around 1850. It was bought by couple Martin Cove and Paula Hickey in 2019, who were working passionately to renovate the three floors above. The pair have since kickstarted a fundraising campaign to restore the building soon after the fire, because the mill was uninsurable. Martin and Paula said the blaze ’caused the almost total loss of the main mill structure’. “No one was injured, and for that we are incredibly thankful,” the couple said at the time of the fire. “But we are heartbroken at the loss of not only our beloved Lodge Mill, but also the homes of the many local businesses and the community space we had all built together. “The outpouring of love and compassion from the people of Middleton and the surrounding area has given us the strength to carry on.” The GoFundMe page has raised just over £7,000 since it was launched six months ago. Thanks to a group of keen volunteers, life has returned to the mill. Rubble has been moved from the old Engine Room and more than 120 pallets of full bricks, Yorkshire Stone and specialty bricks have been picked up by hand and stacked. The annual duck race was held at the site in May, the ice cream shop has reopened and there are upcoming events for Halloween and Christmas. There is a long-term vision to bring the mill back into proper use again, with businesses on the ground floor and new flats above. But before that can happen, the site needs to be cleared. One keen volunteer is Dawn Alker, she visited The Ice Cream Shop at Lodge around eight years ago. She has returned many times since, but most recently as a volunteer. She said: “I went there for ice cream about seven or eight years ago and fell in love with the place. When it burnt down they asked for volunteers to clean it up. “Everyone goes down and chips in and does what they can on the day. “I used to be a manager in the NHS and now I am making a monster for Halloween in a burnt down mill. “It’s really nice to be working collectively. It’s turned into a community support project in a way. “I have mental health issues and I had stopped going outside and stayed inside too much. I started helping, selfishly, because I wanted the ice cream place back open again. “My mental health started to improve as I got moving more and others have said the same. “In terms of the project we have got to clear the site because it was bulldozed. Then the end goal is to rebuild it. “Then we want small businesses with flats over the top of them. That is just a vision at the moment. “It is going to  be a long project but it is going to be brilliant.” Dawn went on to say that the managers of Lodge Mill, Martin and Paula, have already instructed architects and looked at the structural integrity of the remaining walls at the mill. The business owners are hoping to submit planning proposals to the council in the coming months. articles.title: From six modems to 580 staff: Rochdale’s Zen Internet puts people and planet alongside profit
articles.excerpt: Rochdale’s Zen Internet grew from £5,000 and six dial-up modems into a national broadband provider. Its B Corp approach puts customers, staff and the environment alongside profit.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale broadband business that began with £5,000 and six dial-up modems is highlighting how its B Corp approach shapes decisions about customers, staff and the environment.

Zen Internet was founded in 1995 after a conversation over a couple of pints between brothers Richard and Daniel Tang. Today, the company employs 580 people and supplies connectivity to homes and businesses across the UK.

Alongside that growth, Zen has retained its independence. Founder and chief executive Richard Tang remains its sole shareholder and has pledged never to sell the company.

What does being a B Corp mean?

Zen became a Certified B Corporation in 2020, joining a movement of businesses assessed against B Lab’s standards of social and environmental performance, transparency and accountability.

For Zen, that means considering the impact of its decisions on employees, customers, communities and the environment alongside financial performance.

The company points to practical examples, including two paid volunteering days each year for every employee, a fully UK based customer service team and a Contract Price Promise offering no mid-contract price rises.

Its community support includes donations to charities chosen through staff votes, involvement in the Rochdale Ambassadors scheme to attract investment and support for Rochdale Circle, which helps older residents live independently.

Zen also says it reinvests profits in its network and services, uses 100% renewable energy and refurbishes routers to extend their working lives and reduce waste.

One sourcing decision involved choosing an alternative to planned solar panels after identifying modern slavery concerns in the supply chain, despite the additional cost.

A business built for the long term

Tang says the company’s independence gives it freedom to make decisions with lasting benefits.

“From the moment I started Zen, I wanted to build a company that made a positive difference to the wider world, not just the bottom line,” he said.

“Becoming a B Corp was a natural fit given our freedom to make long-term choices, like keeping our support team in the UK and never raising prices mid-contract, that a purely shareholder-first business might struggle to justify.”

For Rochdale, Zen’s story is also one of a locally founded company growing into a national provider while continuing to employ hundreds of people.

For customers, the practical questions are straightforward: how much will a service cost over the full contract, who will answer when something goes wrong, and what happens to equipment when it is replaced?

Zen’s approach puts those everyday concerns at the centre of its business story.

articles.title: Plans for 17-storey tower next to historic Marble Arch pub rejected
articles.excerpt: Councillors have rejected a proposal for a 17-storey tower block beside the Grade II-listed Marble Arch pub in Manchester, citing concerns over its impact on the historic site.
articles.content_html:
Plans for a 17-storey tower block next to the historic Marble Arch pub have been rejected by Manchester City Council's planning committee. The proposal, submitted by The McGoff Group, aimed to construct 153 flats adjacent to the Grade II-listed pub on Rochdale Road, which has been serving customers since 1888.

The pub's owners expressed concerns that the development would threaten its future, describing the proposed building as "overbearing and oppressive".

Councillor Jon-Connor Lyons voiced his worries about the potential impact on "one of Manchester's distinctive and much-loved historic pubs", highlighting the importance of preserving the pub's setting.

In addition to the concerns raised about the Marble Arch, councillors noted the absence of affordable housing in the proposed development as a significant factor in their decision to refuse the application. The committee's rejection reflects a growing awareness of the need to balance urban development with the preservation of historical sites.

The Marble Arch pub remains a key landmark in the community, and its protection is seen as vital for preserving local heritage.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Rejects Takeaway Application on Health Grounds
articles.excerpt: Plans for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street in Rochdale have been rejected by the council due to concerns over public health and the existing number of fast-food outlets in the area.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has refused an application for a new takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street, citing health concerns related to the high number of existing fast-food establishments in the area. The proposal, submitted by Sheeraz Ahmed, aimed to convert the former Ria Money Transfer shop into a takeaway primarily focused on collection and delivery.

The application detailed plans for a business serving a variety of hot food products, including burgers, fried chicken, pizzas, kebabs, desserts, waffles, and milkshakes. It included internal alterations to create customer serving areas, food preparation spaces, and cooking facilities. The proposed opening hours were set from 11am to 11pm, and the establishment was expected to create four new jobs.

However, the council's planning officer raised concerns regarding the potential impact on local eating habits. The Public Health officer noted that the application would increase the availability of food high in fat, salt, and sugar. Furthermore, it was highlighted that a health impact assessment had not been conducted, leading to the recommendation that the development should not be approved.

This decision reflects ongoing efforts by Rochdale Council to manage the proliferation of fast-food outlets in the town centre, aiming to promote healthier eating habits among residents. The refusal of this application may influence future proposals for similar establishments in the area.

articles.title: Martlet Kitchen in Rochdale wins prestigious international award
articles.excerpt: The Martlet Kitchen, located in Rochdale Town Hall, has been awarded the Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Award for 2026, recognising its commitment to quality and customer satisfaction.
articles.content_html:
The Martlet Kitchen, situated within the historic Rochdale Town Hall, has received the prestigious Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Award for 2026.

This accolade is granted to establishments that consistently earn positive reviews from customers, placing them among the top 10 per cent of listings on the popular review platform.

Opened in 2024 and led by chef Darren Parkinson, who trained at Hopwood Hall College, the restaurant has quickly established a reputation for serving high-quality British cuisine. Parkinson, who has previously worked at notable venues such as Shibden Mill Inn in Halifax and the Fleece Inn in Ripponden, emphasised the importance of using local ingredients, sourcing supplies from nearby businesses like Jacksons Farm in Milnrow and Defiance Distillery at Spotland Mill.

Restaurant manager Sarah Crabtree highlighted the team's dedication to providing a consistent dining experience, noting that the menu is regularly updated while retaining classic dishes like fish and chips.

The Martlet Kitchen offers breakfast and lunch services, along with a grill club on Fridays and fine dining on Saturday evenings. Private dining options are available in the Mayor’s reception room at the Grade I listed town hall.

As the restaurant aims for further accolades in the future, local residents and visitors alike can look forward to enjoying a dining experience that prioritises excellent service and locally sourced ingredients.

The award honours businesses which consistently receive great reviews, with their scores placing them in the top 10 per cent of all establishments registered on the popular review site.
