It’s not the first time the restaurant, which specialises in traditional, high-quality British food, has been lauded. In his food column for The Guardian, legendary food critic Jay Rayner, described the Martlet Kitchen as a ‘victory of professionalism, good sense and, most of all, great taste and skill’ when he visited shortly after its opening in 2024. The Martlet Kitchen is helmed by multi award winning chef, Darren Parkinson, who trained at Hopwood Hall College before working at acclaimed establishments including Shibden Mill Inn in Halifax and the Fleece Inn in Ripponden, both of which boast 2 AA rosettes. Rooted in the community, its food and drink is sourced from the local area, including Milnrow’s Jacksons Farm, Defiance Distillery at Spotland Mill and Grandpa Greene’s in Oldham. Commenting on the win, Darren said: “This award is great news and we’re aiming for more accolades in the future. It’s about good old fashioned British grub, cooked to perfection, using top quality local ingredients, coupled with excellent service.” Restaurant Manager, Sarah Crabtree, said: “I’m so proud of what we’ve achieved. I think one of the keys to the Martlet’s success is that we change the menu regularly to keep it fresh and seasonal, but we also keep the old favourites that people particularly enjoy, like fish and chips. Everyone who works here takes huge pride in their job, so the experience for the customers is really consistent. You know you will get excellent service and food every time you come in.” As well as breakfast and lunch, the Martlet Kitchen offers a fine dining experience on Saturday nights and a Friday grill club. The venue’s unique setting in the Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall has also enabled it to offer unique experiences, with a recently launched private dining offer giving guests the chance to dine in the Mayor’s reception room. Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and culture, said: “When we spearheaded the restoration of the town hall, with the support for the National Lottery Heritage Fund, we wanted every part of its operation to live up to this building’s grandeur and The Martlet Kitchen has delivered this in spades. To have our visitors place it among the top restaurants in operation is incredibly special and long may people enjoy this wonderful place.” Related content Councillor Sue Smith Council news from across the borough of Rochdale The Martlet Kitchen Was this page helpful? articles.title: Chris Cheap appointed managing director of Northern Gateway regeneration in Bury and Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Chris Cheap has been appointed managing director of the development corporation overseeing the Northern Gateway regeneration programme, which aims to enhance infrastructure and housing in Bury and Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Chris Cheap has been appointed as the managing director of the development corporation responsible for the Northern Gateway regeneration programme, which spans Bury and Rochdale. This initiative aims to coordinate the development of new homes, employment spaces, and infrastructure improvements in the area.

Mr Cheap joins the Atom Valley Northern Gateway Mayoral Development Corporation after nearly 23 years at Avison Young, where he led the UK transactional team. His extensive experience in real estate is expected to be pivotal in driving the regeneration efforts forward.

He stated that successful delivery will require collaboration between public and private sectors.

One of the key projects under the Northern Gateway programme includes enhancing road connections to the M66 and M60 motorways, which is intended to facilitate further development and improve traffic flow in the region.

This project is part of a broader strategy to boost economic growth and infrastructure in the Atom Valley Mayoral Development Zone, which also includes areas of Oldham.

The appointment of Mr Cheap is seen as a significant step towards revitalising the local economy and improving living conditions in Bury and Rochdale. As the project progresses, local residents and businesses can expect updates on developments and opportunities arising from this regeneration initiative.

articles.title: Rochdale house prices rise to £211,000 in August 2026
articles.excerpt: The average house price in Rochdale increased by 3.3% over the past year, while private rents saw a significant rise of 8.8%, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics.
articles.content_html:
The average house price in Rochdale reached £211,000 in August 2026, reflecting a 3.3% increase from the previous year, according to data released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

This rise is notably higher than the average increase of 2.2% observed across the North West during the same period.

In addition to house prices, private rents in Rochdale also saw a substantial increase, with the average rent climbing to £859 in September 2026.

This marks an annual rise of 8.8%, compared to £790 in September 2025, again outpacing the North West's average increase of 5.7%.

For first-time buyers, the average price paid for a home was £191,000 in August 2026, which is a 3.4% increase from the previous year's average of £184,000.

Homes purchased with a mortgage had an average price of £215,000, also reflecting a 3.3% rise from £208,000 in August 2025.

These figures indicate a continuing trend of rising housing costs in Rochdale, which may impact affordability for local residents. The ONS advises that local housing data can be more variable due to the smaller number of properties involved, and they recommend looking at trends over a longer period for a clearer picture.

articles.title: Venus Lounge in Heywood wins Restaurant of the Year at National Curry Awards 2026
articles.excerpt: The Venus Lounge has been awarded Restaurant of the Year at the National Curry Awards 2026, recognising its contribution to the UK curry industry.
articles.content_html:
The Venus Lounge, a local restaurant in Heywood, has been awarded Restaurant of the Year at the prestigious National Curry Awards 2026. The awards ceremony took place yesterday at the House of Lords, celebrating the best in the UK's curry industry.

Organised by the Asian Catering Federation, the National Curry Awards highlight talented chefs and restaurants across the country. The Venus Lounge received a crystal trophy in recognition of its excellence and popularity among diners.

In a statement following the award, the Venus Lounge expressed gratitude to its customers for their support and for voting for them. The restaurant's success reflects its commitment to quality and service in the competitive culinary landscape.

The Venus Lounge was crowned Restaurant of the Year at the National Curry Awards 2026, held yesterday at the House of Lords. The honour comes a year after it scooped the award for Manchester’s Asian Restaurant Of The Year at the 9th Asian International Restaurant Awards, organised by the Asian Catering Federation. The National Curry Awards has been established to celebrate and highlights the success of the UK’s curry industry, as well as highlighting its creative and talented chefs. The Venus Lounge shared: “With immense gratitude and joy, we are proud to announce that Venus Lounge has been awarded Restaurant of the Year at the National Curry Awards 2026, presented at the prestigious House of Lords, Palace of Westminster, London! “This crystal trophy is not just for us — it is for you. “To every customer who voted, who supported us, who prayed for us, who dined with us — thank you. You backed your local restaurant and you brought this national award home to Heywood. READ MORE: Why the Venus Lounge in Heywood is the best in Manchester Venus Lounge staff celebrate their award with Heywood and North Middleton MP Elsie Blundell. Image: Venus Lounge “From our humble kitchen to the House of Lords, this journey has been built on your love, our team’s hard work, and your loyalty. “This award is for our entire community.” Congratulating the team on its success, Elaine Maria Nolan shared on Facebook: “Absolutely fantastic, so well deserved. Congratulations to all of the team xxx” Lee Rawlinson agreed: “Well deserved, fantastic food and staff 👍👍” And Ben Thomson added: “Amazing congratulations to you all every time I go the food is excellent and service is outstanding well deserved 👍👍👍” Venus Lounge representatives were joined at the House of Lords by Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell to celebrate their success. articles.title: Rochdale unemployment claimants increase to 8,775 in September 2026
articles.excerpt: The number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits in Rochdale rose by 270 in September 2026, marking an increase from the previous month and year.
articles.content_html:
The number of people claiming unemployment-related benefits in Rochdale rose by 270 in September 2026, bringing the total to 8,775. This figure represents 6.0% of residents aged 16 to 64, an increase from 5.8% in August 2026.

In September 2025, the claimant count was slightly lower at 8,625, indicating a year-on-year increase in unemployment claims. The latest figures were published by the Office for National Statistics through Nomis, and the September data is provisional and subject to revision.

The rise in claimants may reflect broader economic challenges affecting the local job market, although specific reasons for the increase have not been detailed in the report. The data is crucial for understanding employment trends in the area and may influence local policy decisions.

Residents and local businesses may feel the impact of this increase, as higher unemployment can affect consumer spending and overall economic activity in Rochdale.

articles.title: Rochdale Council addresses concerns over local pub closures
articles.excerpt: Councillor Richard Jackson has raised concerns about the future of local pubs in Littleborough after the closure of The Wheatsheaf, highlighting restrictive covenants that hinder reopening efforts.
articles.content_html:
The future of local pubs in Littleborough is under scrutiny following the recent closure of The Wheatsheaf. This closure has sparked community outcry and raised concerns about the viability of pubs in the area. Councillor Richard Jackson addressed these issues during a Rochdale council meeting on 15 October, highlighting the challenges posed by restrictive covenants that prevent former pubs from being reopened as such.

Councillor Jackson noted that approximately 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies, which often include covenants in sales to deter competition.

This practice has led to a significant number of closures, with many pubs being sold off for alternative uses.

He cited the example of the former Royal Oak pub, which closed in 2015 and was subsequently converted into a vape shop, a change that was later halted by Trading Standards due to regulatory issues.

The council's discussion aims to address the ongoing loss of pubs in the community, with Jackson's motion seeking to reduce the impact of these covenants.

He expressed concern over the cycle of tenant attrition that many pubs face, stating, "We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant."

The implications of this discussion are significant for local residents and pub enthusiasts, as the council considers measures to protect these community assets. The outcome of this motion could influence future policies regarding the sale and repurposing of pubs in Littleborough and beyond.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Town hall fears for the future of pubs | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch Town hall fears for the future of pubs George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 17, 2026 | 10:55 AM Print Wheatsheaf The Wheatsheaf pub in Littleborough. Is the future of the local pub in danger? That’s the fear in Littleborough where the closure of another pub has sparked outcry. A few months ago The Wheatsheaf closed down in the Rochdalian town. There is strong community interest in reopening the pub as a local asset, but a small loophole means they fear they can’t do that. When breweries or large companies that own and operate pubs sell on the building, they can include a covenant that prevents it from being re-used as a pub. This covenant is inserted into a sale to stop competitors taking the pub on the cheap, the latest town hall meeting was told. Coun Richard Jackson brought forward a motion to Rochdale council to address this very issue to reduce the continued loss of pubs in communities. The Littleborough Lakeside councillor told the chamber on October 15: “The reality is that around 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies. They have a history of damaging the industry as a whole. This often leads to tenant attrition. “We are acutely aware of pubs being closed down after numerous tenants have left the building. The point of this motion is to address the churn. “We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant.” The former Royal Oak pub was closed down in 2015 and then sold off and became a vape shop, which was later shut down by Trading Standards. Coun Jackson called on the council to write to the government to block restrictive covenants on pub sales. He said that this loophole means most pubs get turned into shops or HMOs. His ward colleague Coun Tom Besford shared his annoyance that the future use of a community building can be dictated by the business interests of a brewery or company. The pair also credited Rochdale MP Paul Waugh for his continued work on this issue and raising it in Parliament. Speaking after the motion was passed in Rochdale Town Hall, Mr Waugh said: “This Government has already done the heavy lifting on pubs. Since August, the planning rules make it harder to turn a viable pub into flats or a shop, and the new Community Right to Buy gives people the power to buy their local. But one back door is still wide open. “A pub company can sell up and write into the deeds that the building can never sell another pint, and that ban binds every owner after them. Littleborough lost the Royal Oak that way, and I’m determined that we’re not going to lose the Wheatsheaf too. “The minister has asked for evidence, and with Rochdale council now behind us, I’ll be putting our town’s case to him directly.” It is a tough time for the pub industry nationally, with approximately one pub a day will have closed by the end of 2026, according to the latest figures from the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA).  The trade body estimates that around 360 pubs will permanently shut their doors by the end of the year. evidence_sources.captured_text: Download ratings data | title Skip to main content Food Standards Agency - Frontpage Navigation Menu UK food hygiene rating data API The food hygiene rating data published at https://ratings.food.gov.uk are available via an application programming interface (API) in XML and JSON formats. This is a free service and there is no need to register to use it. Terms and conditions apply (see link below), and guidance for developers is available. Terms and conditions Read the terms and conditions of using the data and images. About the data The data provides the food hygiene rating or inspection result given to a business and reflect the standards of food hygiene found on the date of inspection or visit by the local authority. Businesses include restaurants, pubs, cafés, takeaways, hotels and other places consumers eat, as well as supermarkets and other food shops. The data are held on behalf of local authorities participating in either the: national Food Hygiene Rating Scheme (FHRS) in England, Northern Ireland and Wales, or the Food Hygiene Information Scheme (FHIS) in Scotland Data for local authority areas running either of these schemes can be found on the Ratings site: See a list of local authorities running the FHRS or FHIS The scores part of the data is only applicable to scheme type FHRS (not FHIS) and are for hygiene, structure and confidence in management. These scores can be found in part 2 and 3 of Annex 1, A1.1 of the Food Law code of Practice . These scores are then used to calculate the food hygiene rating details of which can be found in the Guidance on implementation and operation of the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme: the Brand Standard and statutory guidance . When a rescore is uploaded by a local authority the scores of hygiene, structure and confidence in management will not be available in the data. Where the establishment is in operation from a private address the address and geocoding data may not be available. The LocalAuthorityBusinessID is provided by the local authority and is unique for that particular local authority data but could also be used by other local authorities. The FHRSID is system-generated and is unique in the data. It is based on the LocalAuthorityBusinessID and the LocalAuthorityCode . Where a new LocalAuthorityBusinessID is uploaded to the system by a local authority, a new FHRSID is generated. If a LocalAuthorityBusinessID is reused, for example for a new registration, the FHRSID will be retained for the establishment. Please note some local authorities use their database as a business database whereas others use an establishment database, therefore some local authorities will recycle the LocalAuthorityBusinessID where others will not. There are circumstances where the LocalAuthorityBusinessID and FHRSID may change, such as local authorities changing databases or where local authorities have merged. Details of where this has occurred can be found on the FHRS status page . Other useful information can be found on this page such as data types for fields. The business types and associated ID's can be found at: api1-ratings.food.gov.uk/business-types/xml Where Awaiting Publication is displayed instead of a rating, this is where the business has appealed their rating, and the local authority is in the process of determining the appeal. NewRatingPending is displayed as true in the data where a local authority has uploaded new data for an establishment which is not yet published as this data is in the notification or appeals period. It will be published after these time periods have elapsed. Where this is displayed as false, no new data is in the workflow to be published. Further information about the scheme can be found at https://www.food.gov.uk/safety-hygiene/food-hygiene-rating-scheme System status Status updates, usage advice and various other pieces of current information can be found at the System Status Page. API guidance for developers The API allows developers access to the underlying food hygiene rating data published at ratings.food.gov.uk . Developers can query XML files to return the geocoded data (longitude and latitude data are provided for food businesses). The XML data are updated daily and can be found below, grouped by local authority. Wales's local authority data can be output in English or Welsh. The API can also be used to query the live system (the data are automatically updated as local authorities upload and publish data) and return data in XML and JSON formats. Examples of how to use the API and information about the API can be found in the guidance document for developers: Read the API V1 guidance for developers (pdf 316KB, updated April 2024) Read the API V2 guidance for developers Images A set of hygiene rating images is available to be used with the API data. The images must only be used in accordance with the FHRS/FHIS Brand Standard and the terms and conditions . Examples of hygiene rating images, and the sizes available, that can be used with the API data: Download new high resolution FHRS badges (ZIP - 1 MB) Legacy online rating images The previous version of the online ratings has now been retired. Please use the images provided above. Score descriptors English language Welsh language Downloading data from the FHRS search results page When you search for hygiene ratings on www.food.gov.uk/ratings , you can download the search results at the bottom of the page. Number of results You can download up to 5,000 results by entering a number between 1 and 5,000 in the 'Number of results' field. If you need to download more than 5,000 results, in the 'Number of results' field enter 5,000, then enter each 'Page number' 1, 2 etc until all results are downloaded. Data formats Data can be downloaded in XML and JSON format. To convert the data into excel format use the following guidance:: Microsoft support page: Open an XML data file to import its data into Excel (Opens in a new tab) To merge multiple Excel files into a single file use the following guidance: Microsoft support page: Import data from a folder with multiple files (Opens in a new tab) Downloadable open data file A complete record of our open food hygiene rating data can be downloaded via the link below. The data is updated daily. You can obtain data for individual regions further down the page, or via the API. articles.title: Emmerdale star Lisa Riley meets shoppers as Peacocks opens in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Peacocks opened its new Rochdale Riverside store on Thursday, with Emmerdale star Lisa Riley joining the celebrations and posing for photographs with shoppers.
articles.content_html:
Peacocks opened its new Rochdale Riverside store today, with Emmerdale star Lisa Riley joining the celebrations and posing for photographs with shoppers.

The actress helped officially launch the branch on Thursday 15 October, cutting the ribbon alongside store manager Claire Kershaw and the shop team. Riley also celebrated the visit on her own social media, confirming she had opened the new store.

Her appearance gave shoppers an opportunity to meet a familiar television face while exploring the retailer’s latest addition to Rochdale town centre.

Customers were keen to get through the doors, with the first shopper reportedly arriving at 6.30am. The first ten customers each received a £50 Peacocks gift card.

The new branch stocks clothing for women, men and children, bringing Peacocks back to the town following the closure of its former Wheatsheaf Shopping Centre shop in 2020.

For residents pleased to see the name return, today was a chance to browse the new shop, meet its staff and enjoy a little soap-star glamour alongside their shopping.

articles.title: Rochdale's Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre set to drive advanced manufacturing
articles.excerpt: The Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park marks a significant step for Rochdale's advanced manufacturing sector, with operations expected to commence in 2027.
articles.content_html:
A major milestone has been reached with the completion of the base build of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale.

This 30,000 sq. ft facility is poised to become a key player in the UK's advanced materials and manufacturing sector, serving as a gateway for innovation and collaboration within the region.

The SMMC is the first significant development within the Atom Valley Innovation District (AVID), a 25-acre hub designed to foster advanced materials and manufacturing. The centre aims to bring together businesses, researchers, investors, and innovation partners, enhancing Greater Manchester's reputation as a leading centre for advanced manufacturing.

The completion of the building is the result of extensive collaboration among various stakeholders, including the Rochdale Development Agency (RDA), Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), and The University of Manchester.

The next phase will involve transitioning from construction to specialist fit-out, with the centre expected to commence operations in 2027.

Since the establishment of the Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) in 2023, over 90 companies have engaged with the initiative, benefiting from access to a national network of expertise and support.

This development is expected to significantly contribute to the growth of the advanced manufacturing sector in Rochdale and beyond.

articles.title: Cozy Market in Milnrow shut down again for selling illicit tobacco
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Trading Standards has secured a three-month closure order for Cozy Market on Dale Street, Milnrow, following repeated violations involving the sale of illegal tobacco products.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Trading Standards has successfully obtained a closure order for Cozy Market, located at 79 Dale Street, Milnrow, due to the persistent sale of illicit tobacco products. The order was granted by Manchester Magistrates' Court and will see the shop closed for three months, marking the second time it has faced such action in recent months.

The latest closure comes just weeks after the shop reopened following a previous three-month closure order issued in June. During that period, evidence of illegal tobacco sales was secured by trading standards officers, prompting the court's decision to shut the establishment again.

Rochdale Council announced the closure on its Facebook page, reiterating its commitment to tackling the sale of illegal goods in the area. The law currently allows for a three-month closure for shops found selling illicit products, but there are plans to extend this period to a year, which could further deter such activities.

The repeated closures of Cozy Market highlight ongoing issues with illegal tobacco sales in the region. Local residents and businesses may notice a reduction in illicit goods being sold, contributing to a safer shopping environment.

The council's trading standards team continues to monitor the situation closely.

articles.title: A kitchen to be proud of this Christmas: meet Rochdale’s family-run SJF Granite & Quartz
articles.excerpt: With 25 years of experience and a reported 124 five-star reviews, this local family business puts craftsmanship and personal service at the heart of its work.
articles.content_html:
With 25 years of experience and a reported 124 five-star reviews, this local family business puts craftsmanship and personal service at the heart of its work.

Christmas has a way of bringing everyone into the kitchen. From preparing the festive dinner to catching up over a drink, it becomes the busiest—and often happiest—room in the house.

For anyone dreaming of giving that space a beautiful new finish, Rochdale’s SJF Granite & Quartz Ltd offers local expertise with a personal touch.

The family-owned business specialises in bespoke granite and quartz surfaces, serving homes and businesses across Rochdale, Greater Manchester and surrounding areas. Its website highlights 25 years of experience and a commitment to quality, precision and value for money.

Behind every attractive worktop is careful workmanship. SJF describes a process that takes projects from detailed measurement and templating through to cutting, polishing and installation—bringing the individual elements together into a finished surface tailored to the space.

The reported tally of 124 five-star reviews adds an encouraging chapter to this local family-business story. Choosing someone to work in your home is a matter of trust, and recommendations from previous customers can be an important part of that decision.

SJF places personal service at the centre of its approach, alongside carefully crafted stone and competitive pricing. It is a combination with clear appeal for homeowners who want their kitchen to feel special while keeping their budget in mind.

With Christmas approaching, now is a good time to start discussing the kitchen you have been imagining. Choosing a surface, exploring samples and arranging measurements early gives you time to consider the details and ask about installation availability before the festive season.

Whether your plans involve a complete kitchen renovation or replacing existing worktops, a beautifully chosen surface can become the detail that brings the room together.

SJF’s showroom at 47 Church Street, Littleborough, OL15 8AB offers the opportunity to explore samples. Its website also showcases completed projects and provides a free quotation enquiry form.

For inspiration, project enquiries and Christmas availability, visit https://sjfgraniteandquartz.co.uk/ or call 07311 133375.

Your dream kitchen could start with a conversation—and a family business right here in the Rochdale borough.

Sources and review information: https://sjfgraniteandquartz.co.uk/ and https://sjfgraniteandquartz.co.uk/contact-us/. The figure of 124 five-star reviews was supplied to Rochdale Daily for this feature; the current total has not been independently verified.

articles.title: Rochdale Council announces new regeneration projects for Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has unveiled a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, including the restoration of Hopwood Hall and the acquisition of Warwick Mill.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, following a recent High Court judgement in favour of the council regarding Hopwood Hall. This decision brings clarity to the future of the historic building, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. The council is committed to funding essential repairs and considering options for its long-term future.

In addition to the Hopwood Hall project, the council has made significant strides in Middleton's regeneration ambitions. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to lead to the announcement of a new tenant before the end of the year. Furthermore, the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be redeveloped for new housing, enhancing the local community.

Plans are also underway to transform the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue that will provide activities and training opportunities for young people.

The council has also confirmed that banking and post office services will return to Middleton town centre in the new year, a move that is anticipated to provide a boost to the local economy.

These initiatives are part of the council's broader commitment to invest in the borough, creating jobs and driving economic growth.

The council has also approved a £15 million support package over the next three years to assist residents facing financial difficulties, ensuring that help is available for those in need.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Borough means business as council delivers more pioneering projects | Rochdale Borough Council Search Search View menu Accessibility and translate Borough means business as council delivers more pioneering projects Left to right: Rose Marley and Steve Coogan, with Rochdale Borough Council Leader, Councillor Neil Emmott announcing new Middleton regeneration projects. It's been a busy and productive few weeks across our borough, with positive news, exciting regeneration projects and innovative services making a real difference for residents in Heywood, Middleton, the Pennines, and Rochdale. I want to begin with Hopwood Hall. The council welcomed the recent High Court judgement, which found in our favour and brings much-needed clarity about the future of this important historic building. While it's disappointing that a lengthy and potentially costly legal process was necessary, we are now focused on moving forward. Since 2017, more than £1.6 million has been invested in Hopwood Hall by the council and Historic England, and we remain committed to funding essential repairs. Feasibility studies have been completed and options for its long-term future will be considered in due course. What is certain is that, once restored, Hopwood Hall will serve the wider Middleton community and continue to play an important role in the town's rich heritage. There has also been a significant boost for Middleton's regeneration ambitions, with a series of announcements demonstrating the momentum building behind the town's Mayoral Development Corporation. I'm delighted that Middleton Old Grammar School, recently acquired by the council, is expected to announce a new tenant before the end of the year. This follows news that the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be brought back into productive use, including the potential development of new homes. Meanwhile, plans are progressing to transform Middleton Scout Hut into a vibrant community venue offering activities and training opportunities for young people. There is more good news on the horizon, with banking and post office services set to return to Middleton town centre in the new year. This is something I have long championed and it will provide another welcome boost for the town centre. These projects form part of our wider commitment to invest in every part of the borough, creating jobs, driving economic growth and ensuring our communities thrive. At the recent 'Our Town, Our Future' event, I saw first-hand the passion local residents, businesses and community groups have for Middleton and their determination to shape its future. It is an exciting time for the town, and we are turning ambition into action. Supporting residents through the cost-of-living crisis also remains a key priority. I am proud of the help we have provided through our Helping Hand campaign, which has supported thousands of older and vulnerable residents since 2022. As global economic pressures continue to affect household finances, the council has recently approved a further package of support worth around £15 million over the next three years through the Government's Crisis and Resilience Fund. This will provide emergency financial assistance, help residents keep their homes warm, debt and welfare advice, housing support, access to food provision and free warm spaces. We are committed to standing alongside residents who need support. This package will help reduce inequalities, ease pressure on household budgets and ensure thousands of people receive practical assistance throughout the autumn and winter months. My message is simple: if you need help, please get in touch. Further information is available at www.rochdale.gov.uk/costofliving or by calling 01706 923 685 . Finally, I want to highlight two important events that reflect our borough's strong and enduring support for the Armed Forces community. On Friday 16 October, Rochdale Town Hall will host a Festival of Remembrance featuring military music, marching bands, speeches, reflections and the Act of Remembrance. It promises to be a special evening and everyone is welcome to attend. Then, on Sunday 8 November, communities across the borough will come together for Remembrance Sunday services. It is always a poignant occasion, giving us the opportunity to honour and remember those who made the ultimate sacrifice in service of our country. For details of remembrance events across the borough, visit www.rochdale.gov.uk/events . Lest we forget. articles.title: Rochdale station’s 33 new flats are for private rent: what will tenants actually pay?
articles.excerpt: The Corner Plot scheme near Rochdale station will provide 33 one- and two-bedroom apartments for private rent. Oak Construction Projects is carrying out the build, with Mansell Building Solutions appointed for the specialist frame package.
articles.content_html:
The Corner Plot scheme near Rochdale station will provide 33 one- and two-bedroom apartments for private rent. Oak Construction Projects is carrying out the build, with Mansell Building Solutions appointed for the specialist frame package.

The distinction between private rent and affordable housing matters. A home can cost less than an equivalent Manchester apartment without satisfying the planning definition of affordable housing. No verified monthly rent or service-charge schedule has been established here.

Reporting describes a six-storey development with four commercial units below and net-zero ambitions. Contractor publicity states there are no allocated car-parking spaces and storage for 38 bicycles. The station location supports the transport case, but residents with disabilities, caring commitments or jobs poorly served by public transport need practical arrangements too.

Healthcare capacity and wider neighbourhood services cannot be inferred from railway proximity. The development’s access, tenancy terms, repair responsibilities and actual running costs remain important parts of its offer.

No verified site-specific adverse legal finding against the delivery contractors was established in the sources examined. The construction package should be assessed on its own evidence.

These 33 apartments are separate from Station Gardens’ 81 houses. Both contribute to supply when completed, but neither should be counted twice within broad station-regeneration totals.

Location: Corner of Maclure Road and Station Road, Rochdale

Planning stage: Construction start reported in spring 2026

Homes: 33 apartments, plus commercial space

Let or for sale: Private rent / build to rent; rents and any affordable-rent subset not established

Land: Brownfield redevelopment incorporating refurbishment

Final planning agreement: The executed Section 106 deed, complete schedules, payment triggers and later variations were not verified. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that no agreement exists.

Exact rents / prices: No exact monthly rent, deposit or service-charge schedule is provided in the reviewed announcement/contractor material or established from council/government records.

Affordable breakdown: 33 private-rented flats; no verified planning-defined affordable subset. Private rent must not be relabelled Affordable Rent.

Funded school capacity: No scheme-specific funded additional school places, named capital project and opening date were established from the accessible official records reviewed.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: Contractor publicity reports no allocated car parking and 38 bicycle spaces; station proximity is existing infrastructure. No funded new bus/rail capacity or accessible-parking delivery commitment verified.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

Research checked 14 October 2026. Advertised prices are snapshots, not achieved sale prices.

articles.title: Station Gardens turns former retail land into 81 homes, but the final tenure mix needs to be public
articles.excerpt: Station Gardens is an 81-home development on former Central Retail Park land, delivered through Rochdale Development Agency with Willmott Dixon as contractor. Its announced funding includes £15 million from the Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund, with completion expected in early 2028.
articles.content_html:
Station Gardens is an 81-home development on former Central Retail Park land, delivered through Rochdale Development Agency with Willmott Dixon as contractor. Its announced funding includes £15 million from the Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund, with completion expected in early 2028.

Announcement material describes mixed tenures including social and affordable housing. The public Cabinet record of 23 June 2026 approves housing proposals in principle and delegates final approval; the detailed report is listed as exempt. The final tenure count and household costs therefore cannot be established from that public resolution.

The transport location is one of its principal strengths. Reusing urban land near the station can provide an alternative to greenfield expansion. That advantage still needs accessible routes, adequate services and clarity on any parking restrictions or charges.

Further apartments have appeared in reporting of the wider site. Their capacity and delivery status should be separated from the 81-house construction contract and the 33-apartment Corner Plot project nearby.

No verified site-specific adverse legal finding against the main contractor was established in this review. The funding and environmental claims should be measured against actual completions, energy performance and the costs residents pay.

For the borough’s target, the relevant measure is homes completed in each year. A funded scheme and an announced start provide stronger delivery evidence than an allocation alone, but are not completed housing.

Location: Former Central Retail Park, central Rochdale

Planning stage: Construction start announced November 2025; current progress needs updating

Homes: 81 houses in the delivery phase; further apartment proposals separate

Let or for sale: Mix including social and affordable homes; June 2026 tenure decision needs full verification

Land: Brownfield former retail site

Final planning agreement: The public 23 June 2026 Cabinet minutes record agreement to the housing proposals in principle and delegation of final approval. The detailed tenure/financial report is listed as fully exempt. A later marketing decision for John Rennie Place is scheduled for 27 October 2026, after this article’s evidence date; it is not a completed decision.

Exact rents / prices: Exact rents, sale prices, service charges and plot-by-plot costs are not disclosed in the accessible public Cabinet record reviewed.

Affordable breakdown: Earlier announcements describe mixed tenures including social and affordable homes. The final numerical split cannot be established from the public in-principle resolution or exempt report listing.

Funded school capacity: £15 million Community Regeneration Partnerships funding is announced for the housing project. It is not evidence of a separately funded school expansion; no such scheme-specific capacity commitment verified.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

articles.title: Canine Country Club in Rochdale launches new classes after passing licence inspection
articles.excerpt: Canine Country Club has introduced new puppy sessions and enrichment classes following a successful animal activities licence inspection, enhancing its services for local dog owners.
articles.content_html:
Canine Country Club, located in Rochdale, has announced the launch of new puppy sessions and individual enrichment classes after successfully passing its first animal activities licence inspection.

The owner, Stefanie, who recently took over the business, expressed her excitement in a message to customers, stating, "I am thrilled to share that we passed!"

The new puppy programmes will be held on Thursdays from 10am to noon, providing a structured environment for young dogs to learn and socialise.

In addition to these sessions, the club will offer one-to-one enrichment classes designed for dogs that may be timid, less social, or older, allowing them to engage in activities in a quieter setting.

Stefanie emphasised that the welfare of the dogs is her top priority, stating, "Providing a welfare-focused program that prioritises the dogs' best interests has always been my top priority."

This initiative aims to cater to the diverse needs of dogs in the community, ensuring they receive the attention and care they require.

Local dog owners interested in these new classes can contact Canine Country Club for further information and to book their spots.

The introduction of these classes is expected to enhance the services available to pet owners in Rochdale, providing valuable opportunities for socialisation and enrichment for their dogs.

articles.title: Rochdale’s takeaway winning streak continues as Tandoori Flames takes North West title
articles.excerpt: Littleborough’s Tandoori Flames is the latest Rochdale borough business to take a regional ARTA title, following wins for River Beal in Milnrow and Wild Ginger in Littleborough last year.
articles.content_html:
First Milnrow, now Littleborough. The North West Takeaway of the Year award has found its way to Rochdale borough for the second year running.

Tandoori Flames, on Church Street in Littleborough, won the regional title at the Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards (ARTA), held at the London Hilton on Park Lane on Monday 12 October.

Last year's winner was River Beal Indian Takeaway in Milnrow. And that was not the borough's only success in 2025. Wild Ginger Restaurant in Littleborough also took the North West Restaurant of the Year award.

Three regional awards in two years, all earned by businesses in Littleborough and Milnrow. Not a bad record for the local curry scene.

The 2026 competition attracted more than 1,250 nominations from across the UK. Tandoori Flames and River Beal both appeared on the North West's ten strong takeaway shortlist, alongside businesses from Bolton, Manchester, Wigan and other parts of the region.

Tandoori Flames emerged with the title. The organisers say their judging process considered customer nominations, online reviews, food hygiene ratings and assessments by a panel of judges. That matters because the award is not based on a single enthusiastic recommendation, or merely on how many people happen to vote.

The Littleborough win continues a striking run for neighbouring communities in the borough. River Beal's 2025 title showed that a Milnrow takeaway could compete for regional honours. Wild Ginger's restaurant award in the same year gave Littleborough a victory of its own. Tandoori Flames has now brought another takeaway trophy back to the area.

The ceremony, hosted by presenter Samantha Simmonds and comedian Paul Sinha, brought together restaurateurs and hospitality professionals from around the country. Rochdale MP Paul Waugh was among the guests.

ARTA founder Mohammed Munim congratulated the winners and finalists and drew attention to the rising costs facing independent restaurants. Food, energy and staffing bills have all placed pressure on hospitality businesses, even where customer demand remains strong.

An award does not tell us everything about a restaurant or takeaway. Prices, consistency, service and personal taste still matter to customers. But these results provide a useful measure of how Rochdale businesses are performing beyond the borough.

And there is something pleasing about where the trophies have ended up. The awards cover a region with far larger centres of population and long established dining destinations. Yet, for two years, the takeaway title has gone to addresses in Milnrow and Littleborough.

Rochdale Daily congratulates Tandoori Flames on its 2026 win and recognises the achievements of River Beal and Wild Ginger in 2025.

We are always interested in a good local recommendation.

articles.title: Queues form from 7.20am as SpudBros Express opens in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Early customers queued from around 7.20am for the new SpudBros Express outlet on Manchester New Road, with the first 100 customers promised a free loaded jacket potato at its midday launch.
articles.content_html:
Jacket potato fans were reported to be queuing from as early as 7.20am on Tuesday 13 October as SpudBros Express prepared to open its new Rochdale outlet.

The takeaway concession, at Manchester New Road, Rochdale, OL11 3PT, officially launched at midday with a promotion offering a free jacket potato to the first 100 customers through the doors. The reported 7.20am start would put some early arrivals more than four and a half hours ahead of opening.

Rochdale Daily received a report of large queues forming early in the morning. The precise number of people waiting has not been independently verified.

The Preston-founded SpudBros brand has built an enormous following online with videos of generously topped jacket potatoes. Its Express arm is expanding beyond traditional high streets through a partnership with food business Taster and forecourt operator EG On The Move.

The menu includes the Tram Classic, with garlic butter, a three-cheese mix, baked beans, crispy onions and Tram Sauce, alongside the Spudfather with chilli con carne, other loaded options and build-your-own potatoes.

The Rochdale concession is part of a wider plan to bring SpudBros Express to 30 EG On The Move roadside sites over three years. In an opening announcement, SpudBros co-founder Jacob Nelson said the Greater Manchester launch felt particularly special given the business's Preston roots.

According to the launch announcement, the new Rochdale outlet is expected to open seven days a week: 11am to 9pm from Sunday to Thursday and 11am to 10pm on Fridays and Saturdays. Opening-day trading began at noon.

More information about the menu and locations is available at the official SpudBros Express website, www.spudbrosexpress.com.

articles.excerpt: Thirty-four businesses and people are finalists across 12 categories, with the winners named at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 13 November.
articles.content_html:
Thirty-four borough businesses and people are finalists in this year's Rochdale Business Awards, with the winners to be named at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 13 November.

The finalists are spread across 12 categories. Safe Asbestos Removal Ltd has the most nominations, appearing in four categories, including Business Person of the Year for Ashley Dixon.

Apprentice of the Year: Ryan Ingham, of Holroyd Precision Ltd; Lynne McDermot, of The Willows Dementia Hub; and Conor Weldon, of Salt Separation Services.

Business of the Year, turnover over £5m: First Bus; Performance Doorset Solutions Ltd; and Wheeldon Brothers Waste Ltd.

Business of the Year, turnover £1m to £5m: HY Education Solicitors; and Safe Asbestos Removal Ltd.

Business of the Year, turnover under £1m: ALF Recruit; Life Without Limits Gym; and TFD Sports Club Merchandise.

Business Person of the Year: John Byrne, of Junction 21 Chauffeurs; Ashley Dixon, of Safe Asbestos Removal Ltd; and Danny Simpson, of MID Digital Solutions Ltd.

Community Engagement Award: First Bus; Safe Asbestos Removal Ltd; and The Oxford Pub.

Employer of the Year: Envair Technology; Safe Asbestos Removal Ltd; and Salt Separation Services Ltd.

Independent Hospitality or Retail Business of the Year: Busy Beans Coffee; TFD Sports Club Merchandise; and The Oxford Pub.

New Business of the Year: ALF Recruit; Clay & Glaze Ltd; and Thrive Together Training Ltd.

Outstanding Customer Service: Busy Beans Coffee; The Speech Therapy Centre Ltd; and Wills & Wishes Legal Limited.

Sustainable Environmental Business of the Year: BM Technologies; Pennine Care NHS Foundation Trust; and Wheeldon Bros Waste Ltd.

Young Entrepreneur: Sandro Ballesteros, of Graph X Studio; and Mollie Price, of The Floating Canvas.

Lindsay Noble Hurst, of the Rochdale Business Awards Steering Group, said being shortlisted was a huge achievement, adding that the quality of entries rises every year.

The awards are organised by a steering group drawn from the borough's business community and are backed by local sponsors.

The winners will be announced at the ceremony at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday.

articles.title: Nominations open for Springhill Hospice's 2026 Man of Rochdale award
articles.excerpt: Springhill Hospice invites nominations for its 2026 Man of Rochdale award, recognising local volunteers. Nominations close on 2 November, with the winner announced at a luncheon on 27 November.
articles.content_html:
Springhill Hospice has opened nominations for its 2026 Man of Rochdale award, which celebrates volunteers who make significant contributions to the community. The award aims to recognise individuals who selflessly give their time to help others across the borough. Nominations will remain open until midnight on Monday, 2 November.

To be eligible, nominees must reside in the borough of Rochdale, be over 18 years old, and provide voluntary service for the benefit of the community. Individuals who have previously received a Royal Award, such as an MBE or OBE, are not eligible for this award. The winner will be announced during an awards luncheon at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday, 27 November, starting at 1pm.

Last year's recipient was a man who founded Re-Use Littleborough, a non-profit organisation that assists families in accessing essential items and supports children and communities overseas. In 2024, a man received the award after garnering over 40 nominations for his dedicated work with homeless and vulnerable individuals through the Good Solution Network and local charities.

This year marks the 32nd ceremony for the Man of Rochdale award, which is sponsored by Jackson Jackson and Sons, a local building and construction company. Tickets for the luncheon are priced at £65, with tables of ten available for £650. Proceeds from the event will support the hospice's care for adults with terminal or life-threatening illnesses and their families in Rochdale.

articles.title: Rochdale research centre moves closer to opening with £107m economic ambition
articles.excerpt: The Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park has completed its main building, with specialist fit-out ahead of a planned 2027 opening.
articles.content_html:
A new Rochdale facility designed to help turn scientific discoveries into commercial products has reached a construction milestone, ahead of a planned opening in 2027.

The main building of the Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre, at Kingsway Business Park, is now complete. Specialist equipment and facilities will be installed before it becomes operational.

The centre will support work on advanced materials with potential applications in medicine, electronics and construction, helping researchers test whether ideas developed in laboratories can become practical products.

Scientists and businesses will work with the University of Manchester and specialist innovation partners, connecting research expertise with the facilities needed to develop and manufacture new technologies.

The 30,000 sq ft centre is the first major physical development within the Atom Valley Innovation District, bringing researchers, manufacturers and investors together in Rochdale.

Independent analysis cited by the project’s partners forecasts £107 million in economic value over ten years, alongside opportunities to attract investment, businesses and skilled employment. That figure is a forecast, rather than income already generated.

Professor John Holden, the University of Manchester’s vice-president for civic engagement and innovation, said the next challenge was to connect the building with businesses, research and expertise to create lasting benefits.

For Rochdale, the centre represents a step towards establishing a larger advanced manufacturing sector—although its laboratories are still being prepared for the work ahead.

Sources: University of Manchester project announcement: https://www.manchester.ac.uk/about/news/major-milestone-for-atom-valley-as-sustainable-materials--manufacturing-centre-base-build-completes/ Additional reporting and project details: https://www.themanufacturer.com/articles/sustainable-materials-manufacturing-centre-takes-shape-in-rochdale/

corrections.note: The headline has been corrected to distinguish completion of the main building from the centre’s planned operational opening in 2027. The £107 million economic forecast covers ten years.

articles.title: ‘Really nice’: an editor’s visit to the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Daily's editor visited the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with her little girl and found kind, efficient staff, a fully available menu and a welcome that earned a child's verdict: ‘really nice’.
articles.content_html:
There are plenty of ways to judge a new coffee shop. You can look at the menu, the speed of the service or whether it manages to make a quick stop feel pleasant. But after visiting the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with my little girl, I found that the most telling review came from her.

“Really nice,” she said of the people working there. Two words, and a rather lovely assessment.

As the editor of Rochdale Daily, I spend a great deal of time looking at what opens, closes and changes across the borough. This time, rather than reporting on a launch, I wanted to experience the place as an ordinary customer — and a parent.

What stood out was the staff. They were kind, welcoming and efficient, handling our visit with the sort of ease that makes all the difference when you have a child alongside you. Good service does not need to be theatrical. Often, it is simply being treated warmly while everything runs as it should.

The full menu was available during our visit, too. There were no disappointing discoveries that something we wanted could not be ordered. It is a simple thing, but it matters: choice is only useful when the items are actually available.

The branch, which opened in August near Rochdale Infirmary and Dunelm, provides both indoor seating and a drive-through. For people visiting the hospital, passing along Whitworth Road or simply looking for a coffee stop, those options are convenient. But convenience alone is not what makes a customer want to return.

Children have an uncomplicated way of measuring an experience. They remember whether somebody was kind. They notice when they are made to feel welcome. My little girl did not care about the branding or the opening ceremony; she cared that the people were, in her words, “really nice”.

This was one family visit, not a claim that every visit will be identical. But the team deserve credit for getting the fundamentals right: kindness, efficiency and a menu we could actually order from.

Sometimes a new business makes its best first impression not through a grand announcement but through the people behind the counter. On our visit to Whitworth Road, Starbucks did exactly that.

Editor’s note: This is a first-hand editorial account of a visit, not a paid advertisement. For the original opening report, see Rochdale Daily’s article, “New Starbucks Drive-Through Opens on Whitworth Road”.

CTML Ltd is a locksmith based at Unit 1, Arena Court, Mirabel Street, in Manchester city centre.

Its services include lock repairs, from cutting a new key to rebuilding a lock in its workshop when a replacement is no longer made. It also cuts keys for many kinds of lock, including safes and windows.

The company also installs and services emergency exit hardware and wireless intruder alarms, and opens and maintains safes and vaults. It says it draws on more than 90 years of experience.

Its website does not say which areas it covers, so customers in the Rochdale borough should ask when they ring.

articles.title: Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit highlights opportunities for local businesses
articles.excerpt: Businesses and organisations gathered at the Crown Oil Arena for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on accessing contracts, bidding and local economic growth.
articles.content_html:
Businesses and organisations from across the borough have come together for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on how local firms can access procurement opportunities and grow their businesses.

The event was organised by the Rochdale Development Agency and held at the newly refurbished Crown Oil Arena, home of Rochdale AFC.

The summit brought together organisations involved in procurement, regeneration and business support, including STAR Procurement, Match My Project, Hopwood Hall College, Willmott Dixon and the Rochdale Development Agency.

Discussions focused on how businesses can get onto the procurement ladder, understand the bidding process and position themselves to compete for contracts and opportunities with larger organisations.

Mayor Faisal Rana, who attended the event, said greater collaboration between local businesses and organisations delivering investment across the borough was important to ensuring local firms can benefit from upcoming opportunities.

He highlighted figures from the Rochdale Development Agency's latest independent economic impact assessment, which it says found that its work had created, supported or safeguarded 765 jobs and supported 699 businesses. The assessment also reported £14.30 in local economic value for every £1 invested.

The mayor also pointed to major investment programmes including Atom Valley, the Rochdale Rail Corridor, town centre regeneration, housing and skills investment as areas where businesses could potentially benefit from future procurement and supply-chain opportunities.

The summit comes as public-sector and regeneration projects continue to create demand for contractors, suppliers and other local businesses across a range of sectors.

The Rochdale Development Agency and organisations involved in procurement are encouraging businesses to understand the opportunities available and build their capacity to bid for work.

The event also underlined the potential economic impact of keeping a greater share of investment within the local economy, through jobs, business growth and local supply chains.

The Rochdale AFC Community Trust was also associated with the event.

articles.title: From historic chapel to bridal sanctuary: Orla Bridal celebrates its launch in Mytholmroyd
articles.excerpt: A new independent bridal boutique has opened in one of Mytholmroyd’s historic buildings, bringing a new chapter of celebration to The Chapel on Scout Road.
articles.content_html:
A new independent bridal boutique has opened in one of Mytholmroyd’s historic buildings, bringing a fresh chapter of celebration to The Chapel on Scout Road.

Founded by Littleborough businesswomen Jessica Demain and Delphine Gott, Orla Bridal marked its launch on Saturday 3 October with a celebration attended by family, friends and local businesses who helped bring their vision to life.

The pair have created a warm, welcoming bridal sanctuary, combining the building’s character with sparkling chandeliers, thoughtful interiors and a collection of designer gowns from Justin Alexander, Madi Lane and Modeca. Visits are private and by appointment only, giving each bride the space and personal attention to enjoy finding her dress with her closest guests.

Originally built in 1806, the Methodist chapel was extended to accommodate a Sunday school in 1872. Acquired by The Craggs Country Business Parks in 2018, it was sensitively restored and transformed into offices, preserving its heritage for a new generation.

Now, Orla is bringing something of the building’s original spirit back to its rooms: a place to gather, share meaningful moments and celebrate love.

For Jess and Delphine, that sense of occasion and belonging is at the heart of the business. Their vision is for every bride to feel comfortable, celebrated and free to be herself, surrounded by beautiful dresses in a calm and supportive setting.

Saturday’s launch offered guests a first look at the boutique, with flowers, fizz and cakes marking the culmination of weeks of preparation and support from local makers, tradespeople and businesses.

Orla Bridal is now welcoming appointment bookings at The Chapel, Scout Road, Mytholmroyd.

Visit www.orlabridal.com or follow @orla.bridal on Instagram.

articles.title: One in seven Rochdale businesses could be overpaying business rates, research claims
articles.excerpt: More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to BusinessRateChecker.com.
articles.content_html:
More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to research from business rates intelligence company BusinessRateChecker.com.

The company's analysis examined 8,607 commercial properties in the borough and flagged 1,308 — 15.2% — as potentially over-assessed.

That was the highest proportion of any English local authority area included in BusinessRateChecker's analysis, ahead of Maidstone at 13.8%, Kirklees at 13.7% and Mid Suffolk at 13.7%.

BusinessRateChecker estimates the affected Rochdale properties could have grounds for reductions worth around £2.9 million collectively each year, equivalent to an average potential saving of approximately £2,217 for each property it identified.

However, the findings do not allege wrongdoing by Rochdale Borough Council.

The underlying rateable value of a commercial property is determined by the Valuation Office Agency. Councils then use the relevant rateable value and multiplier when calculating business rates bills.

Rupert Spiegelberg, CEO of BusinessRateChecker.com, told Rochdale Daily that businesses also have a responsibility to ensure the property information being used is accurate.

He said: “It is actually the responsibility of the property owner to update the VOA with changes in details of floor space, floor usage etc. Different RVs are applied to different spaces in a property. Many don't.”

He said larger companies were generally more likely to scrutinise their valuations because they had the resources to employ professional surveyors, while smaller businesses could be less likely to question what they were being charged.

He added: “Large businesses are usually quite up on this and will have the resources to hire surveyors to help them but for smaller businesses like hairdressers, coffee shops etc they tend not to question the bills as much.”

How Rochdale properties were assessed

BusinessRateChecker says its system compares the rate per square metre and zoning rates of individual properties with comparable nearby premises in the same category and valuation scheme.

It then examines factors including comparable rateable values and floor areas to identify properties whose valuations appear materially different from similar premises.

The company says tolerance bands are included to avoid flagging marginal cases.

Spiegelberg also told Rochdale Daily that the 1,308 figure could be an underestimate because some properties cannot be reliably assessed by its system.

Pubs are one example because valuations can depend partly on trading information which BusinessRateChecker does not have access to.

The company's own Rochdale dataset consequently records some properties as unassessable rather than assuming they are being charged correctly.

BusinessRateChecker currently analyses around 1.9 million commercial properties across England, using the published VOA rating list alongside other data to identify properties which may warrant further investigation.

Businesses can check their own property against comparable premises through the company's online checker.

BusinessRateChecker.com — check a property: https://www.businessratechecker.com/check

Source: BusinessRateChecker.com / information supplied directly to Rochdale Daily by CEO Rupert Spiegelberg.

articles.title: £12m plan aims to bring Storage World Middleton site back to life after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: A £12m rebirth bid has been launched for the Storage World site in Middleton, more than a year after a devastating fire destroyed the Old Hall Street facility.
articles.content_html:
A £12m bid to bring the Storage World site in Middleton back to life has been launched, marking a major potential investment in an important part of the town centre following last year's devastating fire.

The proposals concern the Storage World site on Old Hall Street, next to Middleton Arena. The former storage facility was badly damaged by a major blaze in June 2025, which burned for several days and led to demolition of the building. No injuries were reported, although customers and businesses suffered significant losses.

Place North West has reported that Storage World has now launched a £12m rebirth bid for the site. The move comes as regeneration work and planning for the wider Middleton town centre area continues.

Official Rochdale Development Agency updates show that the council and RDA have remained in discussions with Storage World since the fire. In June, the RDA said it was working with stakeholders to develop key principles for the area, including the potential to deliver improvements to Middleton Arena and create a new public space. It also confirmed that discussions with Storage World were continuing with input from Rochdale Borough Council's planning team.

The site is particularly significant because of its position beside Middleton Arena and within an area being considered as part of wider plans for the future of Middleton town centre. Earlier council reports said the outcomes of discussions over Storage World and the arena would feed into wider masterplanning work.

Before the fire, Storage World operated a large self-storage and workspace facility from Old Hall Street. The Middleton operation had previously expanded as demand grew, with the company providing traditional storage alongside space used by small and online businesses.

The 2025 blaze had a substantial impact on customers. Fire crews worked for days at the scene and parts of the building were demolished while firefighting operations were still under way to allow crews safe access. Storage World said at the time that its team was devastated by the impact on customers and the wider community.

The latest £12m proposal therefore represents a potentially significant next chapter for a prominent town-centre site and comes at a time when Middleton is the subject of wider regeneration and masterplanning proposals.

Rochdale Daily will update this story as further planning documents and details of the proposed redevelopment become publicly available.

articles.title: The Summit Inn reopens with new menu featuring pub classics and homemade favourites
articles.excerpt: The Summit Inn has reopened with a new food menu featuring homemade starters, sandwiches, hot lunches, and salads, with dishes ranging from black pudding stack to braised steak sandwiches.
articles.content_html:
The Summit Inn has reopened its doors with a new menu packed with traditional pub favourites, homemade dishes and lighter lunch options.

The refreshed offering includes starters and light bites from £6, with homemade soup of the day served with bread and butter. Other starters include a black pudding stack with potato cake, poached egg and English mustard sauce for £8.50; chicken liver pâté with cranberry sauce and toast for £8; garlic mushrooms on toasted sourdough for £8.50; lamb koftas with roasted red pepper houmous and pitta for £8.50; traditional prawn cocktail for £8.50; Cajun chicken skewers for £7.50; and chicken tenders for £7.95.

A selection of cold sandwiches is priced at £7, served on white or brown bloomer with a dressed salad garnish. Fillings include roast ham and English mustard, roast beef and horseradish, roast turkey and stuffing, tuna mayonnaise, and savoury cheese and onion. Diners can add a small bowl of homemade soup for £4 or homemade chips or skinny fries for £3.

The hot sandwich menu includes a classic BLT for £11, while a braised steak sandwich with slow-cooked beef, onion gravy and fries is £13. A triple-decker chicken and bacon club and a tuna melt are also £13, with toasted home-cooked ham and cheddar or cheddar and tomato sandwiches priced at £12.

For those looking for something lighter, salads include a £12.95 Ploughman's Lunch with homemade pâté, cheese, home-cooked ham, mixed salad, apple, celery, onion chutney and crusty bread. Chicken and bacon salad, chicken Caesar salad and halloumi salad are also available at £12.95.

The new menu combines familiar pub dishes with several homemade elements and gives customers options ranging from a bowl of soup or sandwich through to a more substantial lunch.

The reopening brings another food option back into service for residents and visitors, with the Summit Inn welcoming customers to try the new menu.

Menu items, prices and availability may change; customers should check with the venue for the latest offering before travelling.

articles.title: Rochdale brewery brings Retro Range of cask ales to The Baum this Friday
articles.excerpt: Coley's Brewery, now based at Fieldhouse Industrial Estate after previously brewing in Salford, will have three beers from its Retro Range pouring at The Baum in Rochdale this Friday.
articles.content_html:
A cask ale brewery now based in Rochdale is inviting local drinkers to sample three of its beers at The Baum this Friday.

Coley's Brewery has relocated to Fieldhouse Industrial Estate after previously brewing in Salford, bringing its cask ale production to Rochdale.

This Friday, three beers from the brewery's Retro Range will be pouring at The Baum, giving local real-ale drinkers an opportunity to try the Rochdale-produced beers in one of the town's best-known pubs.

The Retro Range is described by the brewery as a celebration of some of the most successful and recognisable beer styles of the past 60 years, combining traditional cask brewing with a deliberately nostalgic approach to British beer.

The brewery's owner is encouraging residents to head over to The Baum, say hello and support locally produced real ale.

The arrival of Coley's Brewery at Fieldhouse Industrial Estate adds another independent producer to Rochdale's food and drink scene and means beer brewed within the borough can now make the relatively short journey from the brewery to local pumps.

Independent breweries have played an important role in the revival of cask and craft beer across Greater Manchester, with pubs increasingly offering locally produced alternatives alongside national brands. For smaller breweries, getting beers onto pumps in established pubs provides an important opportunity to introduce their products to new customers and build a following close to home.

Three beers from Coley's Brewery's Retro Range will be available at The Baum in Rochdale on Friday 14 August. Availability will depend on stocks at the venue.

The event is for adults aged 18 and over. Please drink responsibly.

articles.title: End of the Wheatsheaf: demolition plans would replace Rochdale's empty shopping centre with 443 homes
articles.excerpt: Shut since 2020, the 1990-built centre could be flattened for apartments, townhouses and a new public square linking Yorkshire Street to Riverside. And no - we could find no record of a collapsed Primark deal.
articles.content_html:
The Wheatsheaf Shopping Centre - shut since the pandemic and increasingly an emblem of the high street Rochdale used to have - could finally be coming down.

The centre's Dubai-based owner, DHA Corporates, is working with Muse Architects on proposals to demolish the 168,000 sq ft complex and replace it with around 443 new homes: three apartment buildings and a row of townhouses, on current working figures roughly 134 one-bed apartments, 201 two-beds, 86 three-beds and 22 townhouses. The scheme would also include ten ground-floor commercial units, a community hub building and a significant new area of public space, designed to reconnect Yorkshire Street with the amenities at Rochdale Riverside to the south. An outline planning application is expected before the end of the year.

It would draw a line under three decades of mixed fortunes. The Wheatsheaf opened in 1990, originally linked to the former bus station and the "black box" council offices that stood where Rochdale Riverside now sits. In its heyday it was a bustling complex of five floors, home to some 15 big-name stores and independent retailers, with names like Wilko, Argos, New Look and Peacocks trading there over the years - plus the town's library on its upper floors before the move to Number One Riverside.

The decline was long and visible. Wilko pulled out in 2018 when its lease expired. The centre closed with the rest of the country in the March 2020 lockdown, briefly reopened, closed again that November - and then its then owner, MCR Property Group, announced it would not reopen at all, blaming the shift to online shopping and a retail environment that had become unsustainable. It has stood vacant ever since. DHA Corporates bought the building in 2022 for around £3m, and last year won permission to convert part of it into a wedding and banqueting venue - a scheme that is no longer going ahead in favour of the residential plan.

Readers have asked about a reported deal with Primark said to have collapsed when the retailer was refused permission to trade until 8pm. Rochdale Daily has been unable to find any record of such a deal or any published account of Primark negotiating for space at the Wheatsheaf, and there is no Primark store in Rochdale town centre. We are happy to hear from anyone with documented information, but we cannot report the claim as fact.

The bigger question is what the Wheatsheaf's story says about the town centre around it. The opening of Rochdale Riverside in 2020 concentrated the big names - M&S, Next, H&M, a cinema - on one modern site, and much of the older retail circuit has never recovered. Footfall on Yorkshire Street is a fraction of what it once was, and the units that remain trading lean heavily towards charity shops, discount stores and vape shops rather than the varied high street older residents remember. In that context, hundreds of new town centre homes may do more for Rochdale's shops than another retail scheme ever could: people who live in the centre spend in the centre.

Nothing is decided yet. The proposals must still go through the planning process, and residents will have the chance to comment when the outline application is submitted. But after six years of a dead shopping centre at the heart of the town, the direction of travel is now clear: the Wheatsheaf's future is homes, not shops.
articles.legal_disclaimer: Details of the redevelopment proposals are as reported by the project team and property press; the scheme is at pre-application stage and figures may change. Rochdale Daily found no verifiable record of any agreement between Primark and the Wheatsheaf Centre and reports that claim as unverified.

articles.title: Loombrook Meadows: 302 new homes coming to Castleton - what we know so far
articles.excerpt: Barratt Homes has broken ground on a 302-home development at Cowm Top Lane, with two, three and four bedroom houses expected to go on sale from autumn. What's being built, who it's for, and the affordability question.
articles.content_html:
A brand new development of two, three and four bedroom homes is coming to Castleton - and buyers are already being invited to register their interest.

Loombrook Meadows, being built by Barratt Homes on Cowm Top Lane, will deliver 302 new homes on the southern edge of the borough. Construction began in early June, and the developer expects the first properties to be available to reserve from autumn 2026.

Barratt says the homes will be built with a stone effect intended to match the character of the local area, using modern construction methods designed to make them more energy efficient and cheaper to run. The development is expected to support around 604 jobs during construction.

The developer is pitching the site at young professionals, first-time buyers and growing families, pointing to Castleton railway station, the M62 and local schools and shops on the doorstep. Rhys Nicholson, managing director at Barratt Homes Manchester, said the scheme had already seen strong interest from those groups and encouraged anyone interested to register for updates on the homes available later this year.

How affordable will they be?

Prices for Loombrook Meadows have not yet been released. As a guide, Barratt's other current developments in the wider area list two to four bedroom homes from around £198,000 up to £459,000, and the company promotes schemes such as reduced-rate mortgage products and assisted moves for buyers with a home to sell. Until the first releases are priced, it is impossible to say where Loombrook Meadows will sit within that range, or how many of the 302 homes will be classed as affordable housing - a figure usually settled through the planning process. Rochdale Daily has asked for details of the affordable housing provision and will update this article when they are confirmed.

The bigger picture

The development lands in the middle of a familiar local argument. Rochdale, like most of Greater Manchester, does not have enough homes: demand for social housing far outstrips supply, private rents have climbed steeply, and many working households find themselves priced out of buying altogether. New building on this scale is one of the few levers that can ease that pressure.

At the same time, large housing schemes in and around Castleton routinely draw concern from existing residents about traffic on already busy roads, pressure on GP surgeries and school places, and the loss of open land. Those arguments were aired when the Cowm Top site went through planning, and they will not disappear now the diggers have arrived.

What is not in dispute is the need. A borough of around 220,000 people cannot house its next generation in its existing stock, and every credible plan for Rochdale's future involves building substantially more homes. The test for Loombrook Meadows will be whether the homes that emerge are ones ordinary Rochdale families can actually afford - and whether the infrastructure around them keeps pace.

Buyers can register their interest through the Barratt Homes website.
articles.legal_disclaimer: Details of the development are based on information published by Barratt Homes and local reporting of the start of construction. Prices, tenure mix and affordable housing figures had not been published at the time of writing and this article will be updated when they are confirmed.
